📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By OpenMed, Open-Source Agentic AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR: We built an end-to-end protein AI pipeline covering structure prediction, sequence design, and codon optimization.
  • Imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By OpenMed, Open-Source Agentic AI for Healthcare & Life Sciences.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: We built an end-to-end protein AI pipeline covering structure prediction, sequence design, and codon optimization. After comparing multiple transformer architectures for codon-level language modeling, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the clear winner with a perplexity of 4.10 and a Spearman CAI correlation of 0.40, significantly outperforming ModernBERT. We then scaled to 25 species, trained 4 production models in 55 GPU-hours, and built a species-conditioned system that no other open-source project offers. Complete results, architectural decisions, and runnable code below.

Imagine going from a therapeutic protein concept to a synthesis-ready, codon-optimized DNA sequence in an afternoon. That is the pipeline OpenMed set out to build, and this post documents the process from start to finish.

In Part I, we mapped the landscape of protein AI: the architectures powering structure prediction, the open-source tools available for protein design, and the ecosystem of models from AlphaFold to ESMFold. That was a survey. This is the build.

It has been revealed that at OpenMed, we set out to build a complete pipeline that takes a protein idea from concept to expression-ready DNA. That means three stages: predict the 3D structure of a protein, design amino acid sequences that fold into that structure, and optimize the underlying DNA codons so the protein actually expresses in the target organism. Along the way, we ran extensive experiments comparing transformer architectures for codon optimization, scaled our best model to 25 species, and built tooling that ties it all together.

It has been revealed that this is not a polished success story. It is a transparent account of what worked, what surprised us, and what we would do differently, with runnable code and full results at every step.

Industry observers note that the pipeline has three components, each addressing a different stage of the protein engineering workflow described in Part I. Structure prediction determines what shape a protein takes. Sequence design determines which amino acids will produce that shape. Codon optimization determines which DNA will produce those amino acids efficiently in a living cell.

The mRNA optimization work is where we invested the most effort, and where we have the most to share. The folding and design components use established tools (ESMFold from Meta, ProteinMPNN from the Baker Lab, both covered in depth in Part I). The codon optimization component is entirely ours: new models, new training infrastructure, new evaluation metrics.

Sources indicate that in Part I, we surveyed the protein AI landscape and noted that most biological language models are adaptations of NLP architectures. The open question was which architecture. BERT variants dominate protein modeling (ESM-2, ProtTrans), but codon sequences have different statistical properties than both natural language and amino acid sequences. Codons are triplets drawn from a small 64-token alphabet, with strong positional dependencies and species-specific usage biases. We needed to find out what works from first principles.

The core question: which transformer architecture works best for codon-level language modeling?

Recent findings suggest that this matters because codon optimization is crucial for therapeutic mRNA, vaccines, and recombinant protein production. The genetic code is degenerate: the same protein can be encoded by astronomically many different DNA sequences, but some codon arrangements express 100x better than others. The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID vaccine, for example, was codon-optimized for human expression. We wanted to build a model that could learn these preferences directly from natural coding sequences, rather than relying on hand-crafted frequency tables.

We started with a small CodonBERT baseline (6M params, following Sanofi's published architecture) and scaled up through two families: ModernBERT, which represented the latest efficiency innovations from the NLP community, and RoBERTa, the proven workhorse behind Meta's ESM protein language models.

Sources indicate that the choice of RoBERTa was deliberate. As we discussed in Part I, Meta's ESM-2 (which powers ESMFold) is itself a RoBERTa variant trained on protein sequences. We hypothesized that the same architecture family that learned amino acid patterns might also learn codon patterns. ModernBERT was the counterpoint: a 2024 architecture with RoPE embeddings, Flash Attention, and alternating local/global attention layers, representing everything the NLP community had learned since RoBERTa's 2019 release.

To ensure a fair comparison, every model was trained on identical data with the same evaluation protocol. We used 250,000 coding sequences (CDS) from E. coli RefSeq, covering chromosome and complete assembly accessions. This is a clean, well-annotated dataset where codon usage patterns are well-characterized in the literature, giving us ground truth to validate against.

Our tokenizer maps each codon to a single token: 64 codons plus 5 special tokens (PAD, UNK, CLS, SEP, MASK) for a 69-token vocabulary. This is intentionally minimal. Unlike BPE tokenizers used in NLP, where subword boundaries are statistically learned, codon boundaries are biologically defined. Every three nucleotides encode one amino acid. Our tokenizer respects this.

In a recent development, training ran on 4 A100 GPUs (80GB) with FSDP sharding, using 15,000 to 25,000 steps depending on model size. All models used masked language modeling (MLM) with 15% masking rate, the same objective used by ESM-2 for protein sequences.

Industry observers note that the result was unambiguous: RoBERTa outperformed ModernBERT by 6x on perplexity (4.01 vs 26.24). This was not a marginal difference. ModernBERT, despite its modern attention patterns and efficient architecture, fundamentally underperformed the classic RoBERTa design on codon sequences.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Pre-trained NLP weights do not transfer to biology.

Recent findings suggest that we initialized ModernBERT from its published English-language checkpoint, expecting the learned attention patterns to provide a useful starting point. They did not. Our best explanation: ModernBERT's pre-training on English text instilled inductive biases (subword frequency distributions, positional attention patterns) that actively interfere with learning codon statistics. RoBERTa, initialized randomly and trained purely on biological data, had no such baggage. This aligns with what the field has seen more broadly: ESM-2 and ProtTrans both train from scratch on biological data rather than fine-tuning from NLP checkpoints.

2. Hyperparameter tuning unlocked biological alignment.

Sources indicate that this was the most surprising and practically notable finding of the exploration. Compare CodonRoBERTa-large v1 and v2:.

Same architecture. Same data. Same number of parameters. The only differences: half the learning rate and a longer warmup (2,000 steps vs 1,000). Yet v2's predicted codon likelihoods are 16x better correlated with real biological codon preferences, as measured by Codon Adaptation Index.

Recent findings suggest that the perplexity actually got slightly worse (4.10 vs 4.01), which means v2 is marginally less accurate at predicting the exact masked codon. But it is dramatically better at predicting codons that biology actually uses. The slower training schedule let the model settle into representations that capture genuine biological signal rather than overfitting to surface statistics.

In a recent development, this is a crucial insight for anyone training biological language models: MLM loss alone does not measure biological relevance. Domain-specific metrics are essential. In our case, CAI correlation turned out to be the metric that separates a useful model from a technically impressive but biologically meaningless one.

Sources indicate that 3. The base model is remarkably efficient.

According to recent reports, codonRoBERTa-base (92M params) achieved nearly identical perplexity to the large model (4.01 vs 4.10) with 3.4x fewer parameters and proportionally less training time. Its CAI correlation (0.219) is lower than v2's (0.404), but still well above the baseline and ModernBERT. For teams without access to multi-GPU clusters, the base model is a practical choice that captures most of the codon modeling performance at a fraction of the cost.

In a recent development, in Part I, we described the three-stage workflow that most computational protein engineering projects follow: predict structure, design sequences, optimize codons. Here we run each stage with real data and report what we actually got.

Industry observers note that ESMFold architecture. The model parses a single amino acid sequence through the ESM-2 encoder, then predicts 3D coordinates via a folding trunk and structure module. Figure from Bertoline et al., Biomolecules 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

Recent findings suggest that as covered in Part I, ESMFold is Meta's single-sequence structure predictor. It uses ESM-2, a 15-billion-parameter protein language model trained on 65 million UniRef sequences, as its backbone. The key advantage over AlphaFold 2 is speed: ESMFold skips the computationally expensive multiple sequence alignment (MSA) step and predicts structures directly from a single amino acid sequence. That makes it seconds per protein instead of hours.

Recent findings suggest that the tradeoff is accuracy. ESMFold achieves ~0.87 TM-score on CASP14 targets vs. AlphaFold's ~0.92. For rapid prototyping and candidate screening, that gap is acceptable. When a pipeline generates 100 designed sequences and needs to refold all of them to check viability, speed matters more than the last few percentage points of accuracy.

Sources indicate that we ran ESMFold on 30 protein chains sourced from the Protein Data Bank. These are real experimental structures with known ground truth, spanning sequence lengths from 211 to 519 residues. The set deliberately includes both easy targets (single-domain proteins) and challenging ones (chains from a multi-chain ribosomal complex, PDB 7K00) to stress-test the model.

The PTM scores are solid: anything above 0.5 suggests the model has the overall topology correct, and our average of 0.79 indicates high confidence in the predicted folds. The pLDDT scores are lower than published ESMFold benchmarks, which initially concerned us. The explanation turned out to be our test set composition: the ribosomal chains from 7K00 are part of a large multi-chain complex, and ESMFold (which predicts single chains in isolation) cannot model the inter-chain contacts that stabilize these structures. For single-domain proteins in our set, pLDDT scores were consistently above 70.

Each prediction takes ~10-30 seconds on an A100. The output includes:.

ProteinMPNN architecture. (A) The encoder processes backbone atom distances; the decoder autoregressively generates amino acid sequences. (B) Random decoding order improves diversity. (C) Tied positions enable symmetric and multi-state design. Figure from Dauparas et al., Science 2022, CC-BY 4.0.

Sources indicate that as we described in Part I, protein design is the inverse of protein folding. Folding goes sequence to structure: given amino acids, predict the 3D shape. Inverse folding goes the other way: given a target 3D shape, find amino acid sequences that will fold into it.

ProteinMPNN, from David Baker's lab at the University of Washington, is the current gold standard for this task. It was published in Science in 2022 and has since been validated experimentally: designed sequences fold into their target structures at rates far exceeding random or earlier computational methods. The architecture treats the protein backbone as a graph, where nodes are amino acid positions and edges connect spatially proximate residues (K-nearest neighbors in 3D). A message-passing neural network propagates information through this graph, then autoregressively generates a sequence one residue at a time.

We ran ProteinMPNN on PDB structure 7K00 (a large multi-chain ribosomal complex):.

Here's what the output looks like:.

Recent findings suggest that the first line is the native (natural) sequence extracted from the crystal structure. Subsequent lines are ProteinMPNN's designed variants. At temperature 0.1 (low randomness), the model recovers ~42% of the original amino acids, purely from 3D geometry. This is a strong result: it means the model independently rediscovered nearly half the residues that evolution selected, using only the backbone coordinates as input.

Recent findings suggest that several practical notes from running ProteinMPNN. Scores are negative log-likelihoods, so lower is better. The 42% recovery rate is typical for well-resolved structures and consistent with the original paper's benchmarks. Higher sampling temperatures produce more diverse but riskier sequences. For real design work, the most powerful feature is partial design: catalytic residues, binding site amino acids, or any positions with known functional importance can be fixed in place, while ProteinMPNN redesigns only the scaffold around them. This is the standard approach for engineering a more stable version of an enzyme without disrupting its active site.

Sources indicate that this is where the pipeline transitions from existing tools to our own models. ESMFold and ProteinMPNN are established, well-validated software that we integrated. Codon optimization is where we built something fresh.

According to recent reports, codon usage frequencies vary dramatically between organisms. These heatmaps compare codon preferences across E. coli, yeast, and CHO cells, the three expression hosts covered by our multi-species models. Figure from Kim et al., J. Microbiol. Biotechnol. 2025, CC-BY 4.0.

The genetic code is degenerate: most amino acids are encoded by multiple codons. Leucine, for example, has six: TTA, TTG, CTT, CTC, CTA, and CTG. All six produce the same amino acid in the final protein. Methionine and tryptophan are the exceptions, with only one codon each.

It has been revealed that this redundancy means that for any given protein, there are astronomically many DNA sequences that encode it. A typical 300-amino-acid protein has roughly 10^150 possible codon combinations. They all produce the same amino acid chain, but they do not all produce the same amount of protein. Codon choice affects translation speed (because tRNA molecules are not equally abundant for all codons), mRNA stability (because the nucleotide sequence affects how promptly the transcript degrades), co-translational folding (because translation pauses at rare codons give the protein time to fold), and immune recognition (because the innate immune system in mammalian cells can distinguish native from foreign mRNA patterns). In practice, bad codon choices can reduce protein expression by 100x. This is why every mRNA vaccine, every recombinant protein therapeutic, and every gene therapy vector goes through codon optimization.

Industry observers note that the scale of the codon optimization problem. For a typical mRNA, there are over 10^600 possible codon sequences encoding the same protein. The challenge is finding the arrangement that maximizes expression. Figure from Zhang et al. (LinearDesign), Nature 2023, CC-BY 4.0.

According to recent reports, the classical method is simple: measure which codons appear most frequently in highly-expressed genes of the target organism, then replace every codon with the most frequent synonym. This is codified as the Codon Adaptation Index (CAI), a per-sequence score that measures how closely the codon usage matches the organism's preferred distribution.

Recent findings suggest that CAI-based optimization works, but it is crude. It treats each codon position independently, ignoring the sequence context. It produces repetitive sequences (the same "optimal" codon used everywhere for a given amino acid), which can cause ribosome stalling and mRNA secondary structure problems. And it misses complex dependencies: the optimal codon at position 50 might depend on what codons are at positions 48 and 52, which a frequency table cannot capture.

Industry observers note that we reframe codon optimization as a language modeling problem. Instead of looking up frequencies in a table, we train a transformer on hundreds of thousands of natural coding sequences using masked language modeling (MLM), the same pre-training objective used by BERT, RoBERTa, and Meta's ESM protein models. The model sees a codon sequence with 15% of positions masked and learns to predict the missing codons from context.

What the model learns, implicitly, is the grammar of codon usage: which codon patterns appear in nature, which codons tend to co-occur, and how preferences shift depending on the surrounding sequence context. This is fundamentally richer than a frequency table because the model captures long-range dependencies across the entire coding sequence.

After our architecture exploration (see above), CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 emerged as the winner:.

Recent findings suggest that evaluating a codon language model is not straightforward. As we learned from the v1/v2 comparison above, a model can have excellent perplexity (accurately predicting masked codons) while having poor biological alignment (predicting codons that nature does not actually prefer). We evaluate on three complementary axes:.

According to recent reports, 1. Perplexity measures how well the model predicts masked codons, computed as the exponentiated cross-entropy loss. A perplexity of 4.10 means the model is, on average, choosing between ~4 equally likely codons at each masked position. Given that most amino acids have 2-6 synonymous codons, this indicates the model has learned meaningful preferences rather than guessing uniformly. Lower is better. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 4.10.

Sources indicate that 2. CAI Correlation (Spearman) measures whether a model's predicted codon likelihoods align with known biological codon usage preferences. We compute the Codon Adaptation Index for each test sequence, then correlate it with the model's pseudo-log-likelihood score. A positive correlation means the model assigns higher probability to sequences that biology actually uses. This is the metric that matters most for practical codon optimization, because it directly measures whether the model has learned biologically relevant patterns vs. just statistical ones. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 0.404 (p < 10^-20).

Recent findings suggest that 3. Synonymous Recovery asks: when the model predicts a codon for a masked position, does it at least get the amino acid right? Even if it picks the wrong synonym (e.g., CTT instead of CTC for leucine), predicting the correct amino acid reveals the model understands the protein-level constraint. CodonRoBERTa-large-v2: 12.1% top-1 synonymous.

Putting it all together across our model variants:.

The RoBERTa family dominates across the board. For production use, CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 is the clear choice: it has the strongest biological alignment (CAI 0.404) while maintaining competitive perplexity. For teams with limited compute, CodonRoBERTa-base delivers nearly the same perplexity at 3.4x fewer parameters. ModernBERT underperformed substantially, which we attribute to its NLP-pretrained weights interfering with codon pattern learning.

Single-species codon optimization is useful, but limited. Every organism has its own codon usage biases shaped by millions of years of evolution. E. coli favors different codons than human cells, which favor different codons than yeast. A model trained only on E. coli data will not produce optimal codons for human expression.

The industry standard is to use separate CAI tables for each organism. We wanted something better: a single model that understands codon usage across organisms, can be conditioned on a target species, and can transfer knowledge from data-rich organisms (human, with 145k annotated coding sequences) to data-poor ones (E. coli, with 9k). After establishing CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 as our best architecture on single-species data, we built this system.

According to recent reports, assembling a multi-species codon dataset is not as simple as downloading a few genomes. Each organism lives in a different NCBI RefSeq assembly, with different annotation quality, different CDS boundaries, and different sequence conventions. We wrote an automated pipeline that downloads CDS sequences from 25 organisms, validates them (checking for proper start/stop codons, length divisible by 3, no internal stops), labels each sequence with a species token, and splits into train/test sets with stratification by species.

The final dataset spans three domains of biotechnology relevance:.

The coverage is deliberate: bacteria are the workhorse of recombinant protein production, yeast dominates industrial biomanufacturing, and mammalian cells (especially CHO and human) are required for therapeutic proteins and mRNA vaccines. These 25 organisms collectively cover the vast majority of real-world codon optimization use cases.

A model that sees sequences from 25 different organisms needs to know which organism it is looking at. We solved this by extending our 69-token codon vocabulary with 25 species tokens, creating a 94-token system. Each sequence is prepended with its species token (e.g., [HUMAN], [ECOLI], [YEAST]), so the model learns species-specific codon preferences within a single shared architecture.

This design has three advantages. First, it enables species-conditioned generation: the same model produces human-optimal or E. coli-optimal codons depending on which species token is prepended. Second, it enables cross-species transfer learning: universal codon patterns (like avoiding certain dinucleotides, or preferring GC-rich codons in GC-rich genomes) are shared across all species, while species-specific preferences are captured by conditioning on the species token. Third, the 94-token vocabulary is backward-compatible with our 69-token single-species models, since the first 69 tokens are identical.

It has been revealed that the universal base model is a 311.9M-parameter RoBERTa-large, identical in architecture to our single-species v2 but with the expanded 94-token vocabulary. It was trained for 48 hours on 4 A100 GPUs using the full 362k-sequence multispecies dataset.

Sources indicate that the test perplexity of 24.9 is higher than our single-species model's 4.01, which might look like a regression. It is not. The multispecies model must learn distinct codon preferences for 25 different organisms, each with its own evolutionary history and tRNA pools. A bacterium like M. tuberculosis (65% GC content) uses completely different codons than human cells (41% GC). The model is solving a fundamentally harder problem, and the perplexity reflects that. What matters is whether species-specific fine-tuning can recover performance, and it does.

Industry observers note that the universal base model is a generalist. For production use, specialists perform better. OpenMed's fine-tuning strategy starts from the multispecies checkpoint and trains further on a single species at a lower learning rate (2e-5 vs 5e-5), preserving cross-species knowledge while specializing the model's predictions for one organism.

Training all three priority species:.

The most key result here is the HUMAN model: at 24.3 perplexity, it is the only specialist that beats the universal base, making it our production model for therapeutic mRNA applications. But the ECOLI result is arguably more interesting from a research perspective. With only 8,547 training sequences (compared to 131k for human), the E. coli specialist still improved over the multispecies base. This validates the transfer learning hypothesis: training on 25 species first, then fine-tuning on a small species-specific dataset, works better than training on the small dataset alone. For the many organisms where annotated CDS data is scarce, this approach opens the door to reasonable codon optimization without needing tens of thousands of species-specific sequences.

Industry observers note that the CHO model indicated slight degradation (25.5 vs 24.9), which we attribute to insufficient training steps. ECOLI got 5,000 steps for 8.5k sequences (0.59 steps per sequence), while CHO got 10,000 steps for 42.5k sequences (0.24 steps per sequence). A rerun with 15,000 steps should close this gap. All three specialists fine-tuned in just 7 hours total, leveraging the 48-hour investment in the multispecies base.

After 55 hours of training, we have:.

Sources indicate that all models will be released on Hugging Face under the OpenMed organization. The naming convention follows OpenMed/{model-name} for direct use with from_pretrained().

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-human (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-ecoli (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-cho (311.9M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 (312M params).

OpenMed/CodonRoBERTa-base (92M params).

For therapeutic mRNA (Moderna, BioNTech-style vaccines):.

For industrial protein production:.

The multi-species suite covers the three pillars of applied codon optimization. For therapeutic mRNA, the HUMAN specialist model optimizes codons for expression in human cells, directly applicable to vaccine design (Moderna and BioNTech both codon-optimize their mRNA constructs) and gene therapy vectors. For recombinant protein production, the ECOLI specialist handles the most common bacterial expression host, while the CHO specialist covers the mammalian cell line used to produce most monoclonal antibodies and biopharmaceuticals. For organisms not covered by a specialist, the multispecies base model accepts any of the 25 species tokens and generates organism-appropriate codons.

The transfer learning result is particularly relevant for the broader community. Many industrially important organisms (non-model bacteria, insect cells, plant cells) have limited annotated CDS data. Our results with E. coli (8.5k sequences, improved over base) suggest that multispecies pre-training followed by small-scale fine-tuning is a viable path for these organisms, without requiring the tens or hundreds of thousands of sequences that training from scratch demands.

Recent findings suggest that the full project consumed 55 GPU-hours on 4 A100 80GB GPUs (~$165 at AWS spot pricing), produced ~150 GB of models and checkpoints across 4 training runs, and covers 381,283 CDS sequences from 25 species downloaded from NCBI RefSeq. All models use the same 311.9M-parameter architecture, are saved in safetensors format for fast loading, and run inference on a single GPU with 16GB+ VRAM. Everything is released under Apache 2.0.

The modern computational protein design workflow. Structure generation (top) produces backbone coordinates; sequence optimization (bottom) finds amino acid sequences that fold into the target shape. Our pipeline adds a third step: codon optimization for expression. Figure from Kortemme, Cell 2024, CC-BY 4.0.

In Part I, we described the protein engineering loop as a cycle of prediction, design, and optimization. Here is what that looks like in practice with OpenMed's pipeline. Each step feeds into the next, and the entire computational phase runs in an afternoon on a single GPU.

Consider a concrete scenario: engineering a more stable version of a therapeutic enzyme that degrades too rapidly in the bloodstream.

Recent findings suggest that step 1: Fold (ESMFold). Predict the structure of the starting sequence to understand its active site and identify regions that might be destabilized. ESMFold returns a 3D structure in PDB format, per-residue confidence scores (pLDDT) highlighting uncertain regions, and an overall topology confidence metric (PTM).

Step 2: Design (ProteinMPNN). Keep the active site fixed but redesign the scaffold for improved stability. ProteinMPNN takes the backbone coordinates, a list of immutable positions (catalytic residues), and generates 100 diverse candidate sequences, each predicted to fold into the target shape.

Sources indicate that step 3: Verify (ESMFold). Refold all 100 candidates with ESMFold to confirm they still adopt the correct shape. Filter for high mean pLDDT (>80), correct topology (RMSD to original), and low clash scores.

Step 4: Optimize (CodonRoBERTa). Take the best amino acid sequences and use CodonRoBERTa-large-v2 to generate optimal DNA sequences for expression in the target organism (E. coli, yeast, or mammalian cells). The model scores synonymous codon choices based on learned biological preferences, identifies contextually optimal codons rather than just globally frequent ones, and produces sequences with high CAI correlation.

According to recent reports, step 5: Synthesize and Test. Order the DNA from a synthesis manufacturer, clone it into an expression vector, and test expression and activity in the lab.

Industry observers note that this loop, from hypothesis to synthesis-ready DNA, replaces what once took months of iterative wet-lab trial and error. A researcher arrives at the bench with 5-10 computationally vetted candidates instead of one or two educated guesses. The success rate improves, the cost drops, and the design cycle compresses from months to days.

For a full ecosystem overview, tool selection guide, and license reference, see Part I.

OpenMed is not working in isolation. Two recent models push the codon/mRNA modeling frontier further:.

mRNABERT (Xiong et al., Nature Communications 2025): 86M-param BERT with a dual tokenization scheme (single nucleotides for UTRs, codons for CDS) and cross-modality contrastive learning against frozen ProtT5-XL protein embeddings. Trained on 18M sequences. Achieves R^2 = 0.66 on full-length mRNA translation efficiency, a 1.6-10x improvement over prior RNA models. Code and weights available (Apache 2.0).

NUWA (Zhong et al., bioRxiv 2026): Three domain-specific RoBERTa encoders (Bacteria, Eukaryota, Archaea) with curriculum MLM and supervised contrastive learning. Trained on 115M sequences across ~25,000 species. Beats CodonBERT on 11/13 BEACON benchmark tasks. No code or weights released.

Both models train on 50-300x more data than OpenMed used. That is the primary gap, and we are transparent about it.

Here is what OpenMed does that neither of them offers:.

It has been revealed that species-conditioned single model. mRNABERT has no species conditioning at all. NUWA trains three separate models (one per domain of life). We put 25 species tokens into one 94-token vocabulary and train a single model that can be prompted for any organism. More parameter-efficient, more flexible.

Transfer learning to low-resource organisms, validated. We showed that fine-tuning the multispecies base on just 8.5k E. coli sequences improves over the base model. Neither mRNABERT nor NUWA demonstrates this.

Recent findings suggest that full open-source pipeline. ESMFold + ProteinMPNN + CodonRoBERTa, end to end, with training code, configs, eval scripts, and model weights. All Apache 2.0. mRNABERT releases code but not the pipeline. NUWA releases nothing.

OpenMed is running a proof-of-concept for a fundamentally different approach: Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) for codon sequences.

Industry observers note that standard MLM predicts masked tokens. JEPA predicts masked embeddings. The hypothesis: if the model is forced to predict in embedding space rather than token space, it should learn that synonymous codons (different DNA, same amino acid) are functionally equivalent. MLM cannot achieve this because it is trained to distinguish every token.

Early results from our evaluation suite (JEPA vs. MLM baseline, same data, same hyperparameters, 15k steps each):.

Industry observers note that the synonymous robustness result is the one that matters most for our hypothesis. JEPA embeddings are nearly identical (99.97% cosine similarity) for sequences that differ only in synonymous codon choices. MLM embeddings shift significantly (94.14%). This means JEPA does learn that synonymous codons are interchangeable, exactly as predicted.

In a recent development, the open challenge: JEPA currently suffers from dimensional collapse (91.78% of variance concentrated in one component). This is a known failure mode for self-supervised methods and suggests the VICReg regularization weights need tuning. The architecture works; the training dynamics need more iteration.

Recent findings suggest that this is early-stage research, not production-ready. But if the collapse problem can be solved, JEPA could produce codon embeddings that are inherently amino-acid-aware, something that MLM, by its token-level prediction objective, fundamentally cannot achieve.

Available from the ‘plus’ menu in the prompt box, the old interface launched a fullscreen viewfinder that was quite generic. This UI is still in use when you launch the camera from the Gemini overlay.

This nearly edge-to-edge redesign, which extends behind the system navigation bar, is a stark contrast to the old approach.

According to recent reports, to the right of the capture button is a three-dot overflow button that animates on open, revealing options to control the flash and switch to the front-facing camera. There’s a back button on the other side, but you can also just swipe down.

This camera redesign first rolled out in the Gemini for iOS app, but has now widely rolled out on Android in both the beta and stable (version 17.76+) channels. Be sure to Force stop the Google app if you’re not seeing it live yet.

This follows the launch of GIF creation in the Gemini app yesterday. Powered by Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, select GIF from the Format menu or specify “Create a GIF” in your prompt. Google frames this feature as an alternative to searching for GIFs.

FRSTPM, a completely useless 80287 instruction?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Os2museum

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A reader recently wondered about the details of a documented but extremely obscure instruction, FRSTPM.
  • Industry observers note that to understand what FRSTPM does, let’s first look at its older and definitely useful sibling, FSETPM.
  • While a 20-bit linear address is adequate in real mode (mostly—FP instructions in the high memory area just above 1M would cause trouble, although that was not available on the 8086), it is very unsuitable for protected mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A reader recently wondered about the details of a documented but extremely obscure instruction, FRSTPM. This instruction is documented to exist on the Intel 80287XL math coprocessor, as well as the Intel M80287. The FRSTPM instruction was not present on the original 80287.

Industry observers note that to understand what FRSTPM does, let’s first look at its older and definitely useful sibling, FSETPM. The original 8087 tracked a 20-bit linear address of floating-point instructions and operands, a side effect of how the 8087 interfaced with the 8086/8088.

While a 20-bit linear address is adequate in real mode (mostly—FP instructions in the high memory area just above 1M would cause trouble, although that was not available on the 8086), it is very unsuitable for protected mode. In theory Intel might have extended the linear address to 24 bits on the 80287, but that would still be no good. Unlike real-mode software, protected-mode code cannot trivially form a segmented address corresponding to an arbitrary linear address. The original segment and offset needs to be known.

Sources indicate that intel therefore redesigned the 80287 to be able to track the original segment and offset of floating-point instructions and operands. However, this functionality was to be used only in protected mode; in real mode, the 80287 behaves in a manner compatible with the 8087.

And that is where FSETPM comes in. Since the FPU does not have access to the 80286 MSW (Machine Status Word), and is not automatically informed when the MSW changes, system software has to execute the FSETPM instruction after switching the CPU to protected mode. This instruction informs the FPU that it should use the newer protected-mode format (with a segmented address) for saving and loading the FPU state.

In a recent development, the original 80287 design does not have any instruction reversing the effect of FSETPM. The 80286 can only be brought out of protected mode by resetting the CPU. Intel’s assumption, not unreasonable, was that a CPU reset would also reset the FPU (not doing that could certainly cause trouble). Thus the FPU was reset to real mode together with the CPU and FRSTPM was not necessary.

But then the 80287XL came (in 1990) and introduced the FRSTPM instruction. The 287XL was essentially the 387 FPU in a 287-compatible package. This was presumably a desirable product because the 387 was significantly faster and more modern (much closer to the approved IEEE 754 standard) than the original 8087/80287 numeric core (while the CPU interface is quite different, the numeric unit in the 80287 is the same as in the original 8087).

It is worth noting that although the 80386 can switch from protected to real mode without resetting the CPU, there is no FRSTPM instruction on the 80387. Why? Because neither FRSTPM nor FSETPM is necessary. The 386 CPU (not FPU) tracks the FP instruction and operand addresses, and the floating-point save/restore format automatically changes based on the current CPU mode (real/protected/V86).

Sources indicate that this raises the question: What is FRSTPM good for? On the 386, it has no effect because the CPU, not FPU, does the relevant work. Yet on the 286, it is unnecessary because a CPU/FPU reset is used to switch from protected to real mode instead. In fact 286 system software that is not written specifically for the 287XL cannot use FRSTPM anyway, since the instruction is not present on the original 287.

It has been revealed that add the fact that the 80287XL became available in 1990, fairly late in the 286 life cycle. There were still latest 286 systems sold in 1990, but any system software had a significant installed base of existing 286/287 machines to contend with.

It has been revealed that indirectly related to FRSTPM is the fact that even Intel is confused about how the related obsolete floating-point instructions (FENI/FDISI/FSETPM) work on newer CPUs/FPUs. While looking for any mention of FRSTPM in newer Intel documentation (in vain), I came across a documentation erratum in the Pentium Specification Update. The text notes:.

In the Pentium® Processor Family Developer’s Manual, Volume 3, page 23-37 in the Section 23.3.4 on Instructions, the 80287 instruction FSETPM is described as being equivalent to an FNOP when executed in the Intel387 math coprocessor and the Intel486 and Pentium processors. In fact, FSETPM is treated as a NOP in these processors, as is correctly explained (along with the difference between FNOP and NOP) on the next page in sec. 23.3.6. “FNOP” will be changed to “NOP” in the FSETPM description.

Except even that is wrong! The referenced Section 23.3.6 says the following in the original 1993 Pentium Processor Family Developer’s Manual, Volume 3:.

According to recent reports, the 8087 processor instructions FENI and FDISI and the Intel287 processor instructionFSETPM are treated as NOPS in the Pentium CPU, Intel486 CPU, and Intel387 mathcoprocessor. If these opcodes are detected in the instruction stream, no specific operation isperformed and no internal states are affected.

Judging from the available 80386 microcode disassembly, the above is simply wrong, at least for the 386+387. The instructions are neither NOPs nor FNOPs because the opcode is in fact sent to the FPU (where it may or may not be ignored). And indeed, an updated version of the Pentium manual from 1995 (order no. 241430-004) states the following in Section 23.3.6:.

According to recent reports, the 8087 processor instructions FENI and FDISI and the Intel287 coprocessor instructionFSETPM are treated as NOPS in the Pentium processor, Intel486 CPU, and Intel387 mathcoprocessor. However, the FENI, FDISI, and FSETPM instructions do check for device-not-available faults. If these opcodes are detected in the instruction stream, no specific operationis performed and no internal states are affected.

The updated text matches what the 386 microcode does: The device-not-available fault is raised if appropriate, the opcode is sent to the 387, but the 387 presumably does nothing if it sees the FENI/FDISI/FSETPM (and presumably FRSTPM) opcode. The same 386 microcode path is also executed for FINIT and FCLEX (the non-waiting form in all cases), and those instructions certainly are expected to do something, not just be ignored.

Sources indicate that no doubt related to the general lack of purpose of the FRSTPM instruction, there is disagreement as to how it’s even encoded. Intel datasheets (80287XL, order no. 290376-003, Oct ’92; M80C287, order no. 271092-005, Nov ’92) quite unambiguously list the FRSTPM opcode as DB F4. However, many third party sources claim the opcode is in fact DB E5.

Sources indicate that the opcode for FSETPM is DB E4 so either would make some sense. The Pentium Pro reused the DB F4 opcode for the FCOMI instruction, which somewhat strongly hints that the DB E5 opcode is rather more likely to be correct.

According to recent reports, the book PC Magazine Programmer’s Technical Reference: The Processor and Coprocessor by Robert P. Hummel (1992) is a wonderful example of the confusion. In the FRSTPM instruction documentation (page 676), the opcode is listed (in binary) as DB F4. Yet in the x87 opcode map (page 733), it is listed as DB E5. Take your pick!

The obvious question then is, how do old assemblers and disassemblers actually deal with FRSTPM? But the sad truth is that… they simply don’t. I cannot find any evidence that for example Microsoft’s 1990s assemblers or disassemblers have any knowledge of FRSTPM. The same goes for Borland, Watcom, and Symantec. No sign of FRSTPM anywhere.

Neither is there any hint of FRSTPM in the debugging tools shipped with Phar Lap and Rational Systems DOS extenders. That is perhaps a good hint that in practice, FRSTPM was not used. Which is quite unsurprising, given that it’s entirely unclear why anyone would have a need to use FRSTPM at all!

After much searching, I discovered that Solaris (specifically its disassembler/debugger) has had knowledge of FRSTPM at least since version 2.5.1. Unsurprisingly, the support is still there in Illumos (search for ‘frstpm’ in dis_tables.c). And Solaris/Illumos thinks that the FRSTPM encoding is DB E5, not DB F4 as the Intel datasheets say.

At this point, it’s fair to say that software support for FRSTPM is so obscure that it probably can’t be trusted anyway. So what do we do? Ask a real 80287XL, of course.

To test the FRSTPM behavior, it is necessary to use a 286 system. The reason is simple—as explained above, a 386 CPU masks whatever effect FSETPM/FRSTPM might have. But a 286 CPU should not and the effect ought to be visible.

It has been revealed that the OS/2 Museum has two 287XL coprocessors in its collection, so that wasn’t a problem. But finding a working 286 board turned out to be a challenge. Two previously working boards no longer function (one highlights no signs of life, the other reliably hangs during POST). The third board (Plantron 286A) did better… but not much:.

Sources indicate that luckily, I saved the contents of the board’s EPROM (unusually, a 27C512 chip rather than two 27256s as the BIOS assumes) while it was still working. Sure enough, several bits (three within a single nibble, to be specific) were flipped. So I found an empty 27C512 chip, flashed the old BIOS contents onto it, and the board finally started working.

Even at 16 MHz, a 286 isn’t much fun to work with, but it did the job. I devised a simple test, to be run all in real mode:.

As an aside, I re-learned that the 286+287 needs a little more synchronization than newer FPUs. If an F(N)STENV is not followed by FWAIT, the CPU may access the saved state data before the FPU had a chance to enhancement it. This is not an issue on newer FPUs where the CPU itself (and not FPU) does the work.

The idea of the exercise is to first observe what effect FSETPM has on the FPU (without actually running the CPU in protected mode!), then try both possible FRSTPM encodings and observe if and how FNSTENV behavior changed.

Steps 1-3 behave as expected and need no detailed description. Steps 4-5 are not directly relevant but interesting—the system is put into an undocumented state where the CPU operates in real mode but the FPU is told to run in protected mode.

According to recent reports, the FSETPM instruction clearly does affect the 287(XL) behavior. Even if the CPU continues to run in real mode, the FP environment saved by F(N)STENV is stored in the protected-mode (16-bit) format.

Speculation: The 286 always feeds the code and data address in 16:16 segment:offset format. In protected mode, the FPU reports back these values unmodified. In real mode, the FPU converts the segment and offset to a 20-bit linear address.

In a recent development, executing an instruction with DB F4 encoding (FRSTPM on the 287XL according to Intel, then FCOMI starting with the Pentium Pro) has no discernible effect on the 286+287XL system. The instruction is executed (does not raise #UD) but does not affect the FPU state in obvious ways.

Executing an instruction with DB E5 encoding (FRSTPM according to third parties) does affect a 286+287XL system and changes the format of data written by F(N)STENV back to the real-mode version. Notably the FP opcode is then correctly stored.

Here’s the output of my test program on an 80287XL:.

The last few lines with “Real16” show what FSTENV stores, interpreted as 16-bit real-mode format. The first is after executing FSETPM—expected to be wrong, since the FPU will save the protected-mode version (the Prot16 line indicates the same data interpreted correctly).

Then the program executes opcode DB F4, which is FRSTPM as documented by Intel. The newly stored Real16 state is exactly the same as before, implying that DB F4 did nothing. Next, DB E5 is executed. The last Real16 line clearly indicates that the format of the data stored by FSTENV did change, and the FP opcode is exactly what it should be. This suggests that the FPU likely tracks the FP opcode even in protected mode, despite the fact that software cannot see it.

According to recent reports, it also means that the Intel datasheets have been wrong all along and the third parties have been right; the FRSTPM encoding is DB E5, not DB F4 (as Intel claimed). Executed with DB E5 encoding, FRSTPM does what it’s expected to do, which is changing the format of the data stored by FSTENV.

For comparison, here’s the same program executed on a standard Intel 80287:.

Neither the DB F4 nor DB E5 instruction has any discernible effect on the state stored by FSTENV—exactly as expected.

I noticed that neither FRSTPM encoding or FUCOM (added in the 387) raises an #UD fault on an original 287. Likewise the wrong FRSTPM encoding (later used for FCOMI) produces no #UD on the 287XL. I speculate that the FPU has no mechanism to report an #UD. The CPU clearly does not know which FP opcodes exactly are valid—if it did, the 287XL could not have added support for the new 387 FPU instructions, or for FRSTPM.

In contrast, attempting to execute FRSTPM (with the DB E5 encoding) on a modern AMD Ryzen CPU does trigger a #UD exception.

I was also reminded than on a 286 system, F(N)STENV truly executes in parallel with the CPU. If a F(N)STENV instruction is not followed by a FWAIT, the CPU may access the FPU state data in memory before it has been written by the FPU. This is well documented but the behavior did change on newer CPU generations.

When Intel says that the FPU data pointer is “undefined” after FPU instructions which do not access memory, they mean that actual FPUs do not behave the same. I tested two 287 chips (a D80287-10 made in 1989 and D80287 SX062 made in 1987) and two 287XL chips (one from 1991, one from 1993) and the four chips exhibited three different behaviors.

While looking for older 287 FPUs, I was reminded that the original 80287 was never made in speed grades beyond 10 MHz. The 287 typically ran at 2/3 speed of the 286, but could in fact run entirely asynchronously. For example an 8 MHz 286 would typically be paired with a 6 MHz 287. Some 286 motherboards even had a socket for a separate oscillator used for the 287.

Interestingly, the 287 bus interface was originally specified to keep track of some 286 bus signals (e.g. HLDA, S1#, S2#, READY#). To that end, the 287 had two clock inputs—one was the same as the 286 CPU, the other was the clock that controlled the 287 speed. However, later 287 models (including the 287XL) dropped these pins and the secondary clock input. It is unclear when the information was deleted but it does not exist in the 210920-007 datasheet from September 1987, although it is present (again?) in the December 1990 datasheet 271029-005 for the M80287.

The asynchronous design was almost certainly done out of necessity. The 287 used the original 8087 math core which likely could not run as fast as the 286, or at least was not easy to manufacture in matching speeds. The 80287 was initially only released at 5 MHz, when the 286 could already run at 6 or 8 MHz.

In 1988, Intel released a somewhat mysterious 80C287A FPU which is mentioned in other datasheets but its own datasheet appears to be lost. This FPU could run at 12.5 MHz and was likely derived from the 387SX core. The M80C287 (for which a datasheet does exist, Intel order no. 271092-005) may be a military version of the 80C287A.

It is known that 80C287A datasheet 240347-002 was published in October 1989, but the contents are a mystery.

The 287XL was also based on the 387SX core. While the 287XL is rated to run at up to 12.5 MHz (simply matching Intel’s fastest 286), it is known to run at 16 MHz and faster without trouble. That is unsurprising because the 387SX started at 16 MHz and could run at up to 33 MHz.

Unlike the 287, which can divide the clock by three, the 287XL divides it by two, just like the 286. In a typical AT system with, say, a 20 MHz oscillator, the 286 runs at 10 MHz (20 / 2), 287 at 6.7 MHz (20 / 3), and 287XL at 10 MHz. That alone makes the 287XL perform significantly better than a classic 287.

According to recent reports, the exact 286/287 communication protocol is not yet fully understood; it is not entirely clear what data exactly the CPU sends to the FPU to track the floating-point opcode and instruction/data addresses. The data might depend on the CPU operating mode (real/protected) and may not be affected by FSETPM at all. This area of functionality significantly differs on the 386 and later processors where the CPU (not FPU) is solely in charge of tracking the FP opcode and addresses.

Recent findings suggest that it is unclear if the FRSTPM instruction already existed in the 80C287A. The M80C287 and 80287XL datasheets do not make it clear when exactly the FRSTPM instruction was added.

Industry observers note that another question is whether the 287 really ever used the pins designed to track the 286’s prefetch queue. The relevant information just quietly vanished from the 287 datasheets sometime around 1986.

The Intel 287XL FPU indeed supports an extremely obscure FRSTPM instruction. The instruction is so obscure that it is not supported by commonly available 1990s tools and even the opcode listed in Intel 287XL datasheet (DB F4) is wrong. The actual opcode is DB E5; this has been known since the 1990s and was documented in various 3rd party sources (e.g. Hummel’s book from 1992).

Sources indicate that the utility of FRSTPM is unclear. The instruction is effectively useless because it is unnecessary (a reset brings both the 286 and 287 out of protected mode) and because it is not supported by most 287 processors. One possible use it might have is for testing, in cases where FSETPM is executed without actually putting the CPU into protected mode. In these situations, a regular 287 ends up in an unsupported state which cannot be left without resetting the FPU. A 287XL can be returned to a usable state via FRSTPM.

It has been revealed that fanDuel's US adjusted EBITDA nearly disappeared in the third quarter of 2026, even as US revenue rose 6%. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its Alberta launch, while FanDuel Casino's revenue growth slowed to 8%.

FanDuel’s US business barely turned a profit in the third quarter of 2026. US adjusted EBITDA came in at just $3 million, against $51 million a year earlier. Revenue moved the other way, climbing 6% to $1.455 billion. Flutter blamed spending on FanDuel Predicts and its launch in Alberta.

For the regulated US market, the result shows how much prediction-market spending is costing one of its online leaders. The parent company also lowered its full-year outlook for 2026. Buybacks are on hold for the foreseeable future so Flutter can focus on organic investment and paying down debt. Leverage stood at 4.6x at the end of the quarter, up from 3.7x in December 2025.

Industry observers note that the group’s net loss widened to $1.148 billion from $789 million a year earlier. That figure includes impairments tied to Brazil, where Flutter stopped operating on Sept. 26, 2026.

It has been revealed that fanDuel Casino is adding players much faster than it is adding revenue. Flutter pointed to competition and to slower growth as US iGaming states mature. The contrast with late 2025 is sharp. In the fourth quarter of 2025, FanDuel Casino grew revenue 33% and held 28% of US iGaming gross gaming revenue.

According to recent reports, flutter put that share at 27% for the three months to Sept. 30, the same level it reported for the second quarter. An outside estimate is lower. FanDuel’s iGaming share was 25.1%, down from 26.6% a year earlier, according to Citizens figures published by NEXT.io. The same figures showed US iGaming growth slowing to 12% year over year in the third quarter, the lowest on record.

In a recent development, sportsbook revenue grew 4%. FanDuel’s share of US sportsbook gross gaming revenue slipped to 36%, from 39% in the second quarter. Its share of handle was 33%.

The product drawing the investment is gaining users. Trading volume on FanDuel Predicts rose 102% from the prior quarter to $119 million. CEO Dan Taylor mentioned the app had 140,000 active users in October.

Flutter reiterates $50m prediction market revenue target for 2026:.

Flutter's FanDuel Predicts reached 140,000 active users in October as its parent maintained its $40m adjusted EBITDA forecast for market-making.

Full Story ➡️ https://t.co/B7KSlEgH0a pic.twitter.com/zKXX8fV2fG.

— NEXTpredict (@nextpredictio) November 4, 2026.

Alberta is the other fresh cost. FanDuel reached more than 20% of the gaming market there in its first quarter. Management remarked that was well ahead of its pace after launching in Ontario.

In a recent development, together, the figures are consistent with a company trading near-term US profit for growth in newer markets and products. Taylor took over as CEO from Peter Jackson on Oct. 1, 2026. Buybacks will stay paused until leverage falls to a range of 2 to 2.5 times, a target he set for a period of about 24 months.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision: Compact Multimodal Intelligence for Enterprise Documents

📅 31 Mar 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding.
  • The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines.
  • Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we're excited to announce Granite 4.0 3B Vision, a compact vision-language model (VLM) designed for enterprise document understanding. It’s purpose-built for reliable information extraction from complex documents, forms, and structured visuals. Granite 4.0 3B Vision excels on the following capabilities:.

The model ships as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, our dense language model, keeping vision and language modular for text-only fallbacks and seamless integration into mixed pipelines. It continues to support vision-language tasks such as producing detailed natural-language descriptions from images (e.g., “Describe this image in detail”). The model can be used standalone or in tandem with Docling to enhance document processing pipelines with deep visual understanding capabilities.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s performance is the result of three key investments: A purpose-built chart understanding dataset constructed via a novel code-guided data augmentation approach, a novel variant of the DeepStack architecture that enables high-detail visual feature injection, and a modular design that keeps the model practical for enterprise deployment.

Charts present a challenge for vision-language models (VLMs) because understanding them requires jointly reasoning over visual patterns, numerical data, and natural language, a combination most VLMs cannot handle well, especially when spatial precision matters—such as reading exact values off a line chart. To close this gap, we’ve developed ChartNet: a million-scale multimodal dataset purpose-built for chart interpretation and reasoning, described in detail in our upcoming CVPR 2026 paper.

Recent findings suggest that chartNet uses a code-guided synthesis pipeline to generate 1.7 million diverse chart samples spanning 24 chart types and 6 plotting libraries [see Figure 1]. What makes it so distinctive is that each sample consists of five aligned components—plotting code, rendered image, data table, natural language summary, and QA pairs—providing models a deeply cross-modal view of what a chart means, not just what it looks like. The dataset also includes human-annotated and real-world subsets, filtered for visual fidelity, semantic accuracy, and diversity.

The result is a training resource that moves VLMs from merely describing charts to genuinely understanding the structured information they encode—with consistent gains across model sizes, architectures, and tasks.

Figure 1: ChartNet’s synthetic data generation pipeline.

Most VLMs inject visual information into their language model at a single point, which forces the model to handle both high-level semantics and fine-grained spatial detail simultaneously. Granite 4.0 3B Vision takes a different approach with DeepStack Injection: abstract visual features are routed into earlier layers for semantic understanding, while high-resolution spatial features are fed into later layers to preserve detail. The result is a model that understands both what is in a document and where—which is critical for tasks like table extraction, chart understanding, and KVP parsing where layout matters as much as content. For a full technical breakdown, see the Model Architecture section of the model card.

In a recent development, granite 4.0 3B Vision is packaged as a LoRA adapter on top of Granite 4.0 Micro, rather than as a standalone model. In practice, this means the same deployment can serve both multimodal and text-only workloads, automatically falling back to the base model when vision isn’t required. This keeps enterprise integration straightforward without sacrificing performance.

It has been revealed that charts: Evaluated on the human-verified ChartNet benchmark using LLM-as-a-judge, Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the highest Chart2Summary (86.4%) score among all evaluated models, including significantly larger ones [see Figure 2]. It also ranks second on Chart2CSV (62.1%), behind only Qwen3.5-9B (63.4%), a model more than double its size.

Figure 2: Granite 4.0 3B Vision performance on chart2csv and chart2summary, compared against peer vision-language models using LLM-as-a-judge.

Tables: We evaluate table extraction in two settings: cropped tables (isolated regions) and full-page documents (tables embedded in complex layouts) [see Figure 3]. The benchmark suite includes TableVQA-extract (cropped table images), OmniDocBench-tables (full-page documents), and PubTables-v2 (both cropped and full-page settings). Models are tasked with extracting tables in HTML format and scored using TEDS, a metric that captures both structural and content accuracy. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves the strongest performance across benchmarks, leading on PubTablesV2 on both cropped (92.1) and full-page (79.3), OmniDocBench (64.0), and TableVQA (88.1) scores among all evaluated models.

Figure 3: Granite 4.0 3B Vision’s table extraction performance across cropped and full-page benchmarks (TableVQA-extract, PubTables-v2, OmniDocBench-tables), measured by TEDS.

Industry observers note that semantic KVP: VAREX is a benchmark specifically designed to discriminate between small extraction models, comprising 1,777 U.S. government forms spanning simple flat layouts to complex nested and tabular structures. Models are evaluated using exact match (EM), a strict metric that requires the model’s extracted key-value pairs to match the ground truth. Granite 4.0 3B Vision achieves 85.5% EM accuracy zero-shot.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision can operate either as a stand‑alone visual information extraction engine or as part of a fully automated document‑processing pipeline with Docling. The model is designed to support scalable, accurate extraction across diverse document types and visual formats.

Industry observers note that 1. Stand‑Alone Image Understanding Granite 4.0 3B Vision can run directly on individual images, making this option useful for applications with existing workflows that need targeted visual extraction without modifying upstream systems. This offers easy integration into existing automation workflows and is suitable for lightweight, task‑specific tools (e.g., form parsers, chart analyzers, etc.).

Recent findings suggest that 2. Integrated Document Understanding Pipeline With Docling Granite 4.0 3B Vision can also be integrated seamlessly with Docling to support complete end‑to‑end document understanding. This mode can offer:.

Granite 4.0 3B Vision is available now on HuggingFace, released under the Apache 2.0 license. Full technical details, training methodology, and benchmark results are available in the model card. We’d love to hear what you build with it—share your feedback in the community tab.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, PENN Entertainment's online segment grew revenue in the third quarter, but the gain came from passed-through partner gaming taxes, not from players. The segment now needs a positive fourth quarter to reach a full-year target that has already been lowered.

Industry observers note that other revenues carried the whole of the Interactive segment’s third-quarter gain at PENN Entertainment. Segment revenue rose to $348.4 million from $297.7 million, while the third-party partner gaming-tax amounts booked there climbed to $191.4 million from $139.5 million a year earlier. Online gaming revenue itself fell 2.1% to $126.6 million from $129.3 million, as iCasino growth was offset by lower sports betting handle.

This pattern places PENN within the slowing-iGaming-growth story running through this week’s US operator reports.

In a recent development, the nine-month figures show the same reliance on the gross-up. Interactive revenue reached $1,056.0 million, up from $903.9 million. The tax gross-up within it rose to $562.7 million from $405.6 million.

Recent findings suggest that the group as a whole had a stronger quarter. Total revenue was $1,840.0 million. Net income came in at $32.6 million, against a $865.1 million net loss a year earlier. PENN also raised its full-year retail guidance to $5.89 billion in revenue and $1.973 billion in adjusted EBITDAR, increases of $16 million and $10 million.

Profitability is improving faster than revenue. The Interactive adjusted EBITDA loss for the first nine months shrank to $38.7 million from $227.6 million. PENN attributes that mainly to lower marketing, general and administrative, and labor costs.

Industry observers note that expansion has weighed on the quarter. PENN rolled out theScore Bet, theScore Casino and standalone Hollywood iCasino apps in Alberta on July 13, 2026. Excluding that third-quarter launch investment, Interactive adjusted EBITDA improved quarter over quarter throughout 2026, management stated on the earnings call.

Sources indicate that the standalone Hollywood iCasino brand is central to the plan. It posted record quarterly revenue in the second quarter. PENN is now leaning on its US growth, and on steady trends through October, to support the full-year Interactive target. That makes the brand a test for whether a mid-tier US online casino can turn profitable.

Industry observers note that the target itself has moved. In February, PENN guided the segment to breakeven adjusted EBITDA for 2026, which it described as a $268 million improvement from 2025. The cost of the Alberta launch is now built into a weaker outlook.

PENN Entertainment CEO Jay Snowden discussed the potential of more Canadian provinces launching iGaming on an earnings call today.

In the last month, Quebec, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia have all shown interest in exploring commercial online gambling.https://t.co/8WqAPfw9LY.

— Tom Nightingale (@TNightingaming) November 5, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that land-based trends offer some support. CEO Jay Snowden stated PENN’s own Pennsylvania gaming revenue in October posted stronger year-over-year growth than in any other month of 2026. Most of that growth came in the second half of the month, after skill games were shut down. In his view, the midterm results could help PENN further by weakening support for skill-game machines.

The online segment still has to deliver. Reaching the revised target depends on Interactive turning its third-quarter loss into positive adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter.

Converting Markdown to PDF is easy until the document has real content: long code blocks, wide tables, images and non-Latin text are where most tools fall apart.

Pandoc with LaTeX is still the most powerful route, but it needs a large install and trips over Unicode and emoji unless you switch engines and fonts.

Browser-based approaches (print CSS, Chromium-powered converters, in-browser tools) avoid the install and give you HTML-quality rendering, as long as you control page breaks.

A handful of print CSS rules (@page, break-inside: avoid, break-after: avoid) fix the majority of ugly PDFs, whichever tool you use.

Choose the tool by the document: a quick README export, a long technical report and a multilingual document each have a different best option.

Recent findings suggest that I write almost everything in Markdown: READMEs, release notes, client handovers, meeting notes. And at least once a week, someone asks for "the PDF version". Every time, the conversion looks fine on the first page and falls apart somewhere around page three: a code block split in half, a table running off the edge, an emoji replaced by an empty box.

SitePoint covered the classic route back in 2015 with Creating PDFs from Markdown with Pandoc and LaTeX. That approach still works. But a lot has changed since then, and today there are several ways to get a clean PDF without installing a TeX distribution. This article compares them, then goes through the rendering problems you'll actually hit, with a fix for each.

Pandoc is still the Swiss Army knife. The simplest command is:.

Recent findings suggest that by default, that goes through LaTeX, which means you need a TeX distribution installed (several gigabytes for a full one). The output is beautiful for prose and math, but LaTeX has strong opinions about layout, and customizing it means writing LaTeX.

Pandoc can also render through an HTML engine instead, which lets you style the PDF with CSS:.

Best for: long documents, academic writing, math, automated pipelines.

Watch out for: install size, Unicode handling with the default engine (more on that below).

Render the Markdown to HTML (any previewer, a static site, a GitHub page) and print it to PDF. It's free and already installed everywhere, but you inherit whatever the page looks like on screen: navigation bars, sidebars, and page breaks wherever they happen to fall.

Best for: quick, one-off exports of short documents.

Watch out for: zero control over page breaks unless the page ships print CSS.

Extensions like Markdown PDF for VS Code, or CLI tools like md-to-pdf, render your Markdown to HTML and print it with a headless Chromium:.

Sources indicate that you get the same rendering quality as a browser, plus a config file for CSS, margins, headers and footers. The trade-off is a Node install and a downloaded Chromium.

Best for: developers who live in their editor or want CI-friendly exports.

Watch out for: the first run downloads a browser, and print CSS is still your job.

The newest option is tools that do the whole conversion inside the browser tab: you paste or drop the .md file, preview the actual pages and download the PDF. The good ones don't upload your file anywhere, which matters for client documents and internal notes.

Best for: people who don't want to install anything, non-developers on your team, private documents.

Watch out for: many online converters do upload your file to a server; check before you paste anything confidential.

Industry observers note that whichever method you pick, the same handful of problems show up as soon as the document is longer than a page. Most of them are fixed with print CSS, which works in Pandoc's HTML engines, Chromium-based tools and any HTML you print from a browser.

In a recent development, A 20-line function cut after line 3, with the rest on the next page, is the most common complaint. The fix is to ask the renderer not to break inside the block:.

One caveat: a block longer than a full page has to break. For those, it's better to let it break cleanly than to push it to a newly introduced page and leave a huge gap.

Industry observers note that on screen, a long line in a code block scrolls horizontally. On paper, there's no scrollbar, so it's simply cut off. Wrap long lines in print:.

Tables with many columns overflow the page or get squeezed until every cell is one word per line. Three things help: a smaller font size for tables, a landscape page for the worst offenders, and avoiding breaks in the middle of short tables:.

If a table genuinely needs eight columns, consider whether it should be a table in the PDF at all, or an appendix in landscape.

According to recent reports, A heading alone at the bottom of a page, with its content on the next one, looks broken. This rule keeps a heading attached to what follows it:.

Support for break-after: avoid varies between rendering engines, so test it with yours; when it isn't honored, a manual page break before the heading is the reliable fallback.

Markdown has no syntax for a page break. The usual trick is a raw HTML element that print CSS turns into a break:.

Some converters also recognize a comment like , which has the advantage of staying invisible when the same file is rendered on GitHub.

Industry observers note that images are inserted at their natural size, so a 4000-pixel screenshot spills off the page. Cap them:.

Sources indicate that for blurry images, the problem is usually the opposite: a small screenshot stretched to page width. Export screenshots at 2x if they're going into a PDF.

This one is specific to the LaTeX route. With the default pdflatex engine, Unicode characters outside its supported set produce errors or simply vanish. Switch to XeLaTeX or LuaLaTeX and give it a font that actually contains the characters:.

In a recent development, emoji are harder still in LaTeX and often need a dedicated package. HTML-based renderers handle both far better, because they use the operating system's font fallback just like a web page does.

According to recent reports, internal links ([see setup](#setup)) and external links should stay clickable. HTML-based renderers usually keep both. If yours doesn't, check that headings get IDs (most Markdown parsers add them) and that the PDF engine preserves link annotations.

Put together, these rules make a solid starting point for any HTML-based route:.

Save it as print.css and pass it to Pandoc (--css=print.css with an HTML engine), to md-to-pdf through its config, or include it in the HTML you print from the browser.

My rule of thumb after a lot of trial and error:.

According to recent reports, A quick README or notes export, no install, private content: an in-browser converter. Full disclosure: this need is why I built the free Markdown to PDF converter on AwesomeToolkit, and it's what I use for this case now. It renders real A4 or Letter pages as you type, has an option to keep code blocks and tables whole, adds page numbers and a table of contents, and the conversion happens in the browser, so the file isn't uploaded anywhere.

Documentation in a repo, exported in CI: md-to-pdf or Pandoc with an HTML engine, plus the stylesheet above.

Long reports, math, academic formatting: Pandoc with XeLaTeX, using a font that covers every script in the document.

Something you'll print once and forget: the browser's Print to PDF is fine.

Whatever you choose, the biggest quality jump comes from the print rules, not the tool. Ten lines of CSS turn "it looks fine until page three" into a PDF you can actually send.

According to recent reports, yes. Your browser's Print to PDF works on any rendered Markdown, and in-browser converters do the whole conversion in a tab. Check that the converter processes files locally if the content is private.

Sources indicate that the default pdflatex engine has limited Unicode support. Use --pdf-engine=xelatex or lualatex and set a font that contains the characters with -V mainfont= (and -V CJKmainfont= for CJK text).

Markdown has no native syntax for it. Insert where you want the break, or use the page-break comment your converter supports.

It has been revealed that add pre { break-inside: avoid; } to your print CSS. Blocks longer than a page will still break, which is expected.

With HTML-based renderers, usually yes, both external links and links to headings inside the document. Test internal links in particular, since they depend on headings having IDs.
