Industry News: From formal verification to bug-finding in CHERIoT

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2772 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cheriot

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Cerise project1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University.
  • According to recent reports, cerise started as pen-and-paper proofs about idealised machines and focused initially on reasoning about control-flow integrity of encapsulation for stack-based calling conventions, but over time our research group has scaled up the approach along three dimensions.
  • Recent findings suggest that when I started my PhD, CHERIoT had just been announced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Cerise project1 was started almost 10 years ago at Aarhus University. Its goal is to develop formal methods to verify properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonicity, and to prove end-to-end results in the presence of unknown code. Cerise has been extended to model different aspects of capability machines, and has involved work by and collaborations with several other universities, including Dominique Devriese’s research group at KU Leuven, and the universities of Cambridge and Edinburgh.

According to recent reports, cerise started as pen-and-paper proofs about idealised machines and focused initially on reasoning about control-flow integrity of encapsulation for stack-based calling conventions, but over time our research group has scaled up the approach along three dimensions. First, we made our proofs foundational: Cerise now builds on the Iris separation logic framework inside the Rocq theorem prover, which has been critical to ensure correctness despite the growing intricacy of our proofs. Second, we have investigated how to reason about a wider range of properties, e.g., involving MMIO and attestation. Third, we made Cerise work with an instruction set closer to the CHERIoT Sail model, and verified programs using those instructions.

Recent findings suggest that when I started my PhD, CHERIoT had just been announced. I seized the opportunity to apply the verification techniques of Cerise to the CHERIoT switcher, for example to check that it isolates compartments and enforces no-capture. To that end, we started a sub-project of Cerise, which we call Griotte2.

As part of our verification effort in this Griotte project, we uncovered two bugs in the CHERIoT switcher: (1) the ability for a malicious (or buggy) scheduler to resuscitate an exited thread in a deprecated state, thereby getting access to a capability that it should not be able to have access to anymore, and (2) the ability for a malicious caller to leverage the stack high watermark register to trigger a fault in the switcher, thereby getting access to the callee’s stack frame and thus private data.

The CHERI/CHERIoT threat model includes interactions with unknown compartments containing arbitrary code, which can be buggy or malicious, and which can share objects in memory. Reasoning about arbitrary code is hard, because it requires characterising all the possible behaviours of that code. The challenge is that when trying to characterise what an unknown compartment can affect, we have to account not only for what it is passed directly (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a write capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to overwrite that region of memory), but also what it is passed indirectly—and this involves not only recursive access (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a read capability to a region of memory, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to acquire whatever ability is given by the capabilities in that region of memory), but also access through non-monotonic domain transitions (if an unknown compartment is physically passed a sealed entry point capability to a “counter” compartment’s incr function, then it is behaviourally passed the ability to affect the counter—but only by incrementing it). A unique feature of Cerise is the ability to reason also about the latter part of the challenge.

What makes it difficult to design such a characterisation is that it should at the same time be precise enough, and simple enough to verify the programs that we care about. At a very high level, Griotte defines a language to succinctly describe what is affected—and to state that something is not affected. The kind of properties that we want to describe are not only memory safety properties (if I share a buffer to the caller, then I have the guarantee that it cannot access the global data that I never shared), but also no-capture properties (if I share a buffer to the caller with its global permission stripped, then I have the guarantee that it cannot preserve a copy across calls), and many others (including secrecy, etc.).

Technically, we developed a reasoning system in two parts. First, we defined (and proved sound) a separation logic that allows us to verify known code line by line, showing that it satisfies expected pre- and post-conditions, and that it preserves the expected invariants. We used this both on the code of the switcher, and on the code of specific compartments of interest, for example a key-value store3. We designed this separation logic so it is reusable, and we expect that other such compartments of interest could be verified with it.

Second, we defined a logical relation in separation logic, which is effectively an over-approximation of the effect of unknown code that can be used by the separation logic to reason about a jump to unknown code (through the switcher) in one single step. As such, it works like a universal contract4 for CHERIoT. Crucially, the frame rule of separation logic tells us that if we can establish that the resources (both in an informal sense, and in the technical sense of separation logic) of the caller are disjoint from those of the logical relation, then they will be preserved by the call.

For example, if calling unknown code with a capability to a shared buffer, while keeping some private data, the logical relation requires that the unknown code is only passed capabilities that are safe to share in a technical sense.

We then define a universal contract, stating that if an adversary has only access to safe to share capabilities, it can then execute safely and only produce other safe to share capabilities.

Industry observers note that we started by developing a simplified model of CHERIoT and a mini version of the CHERIoT-RTOS. In particular, we modelled the compartmentalisation mechanisms and the cross-compartment call path of the switcher. Our simplified model mirrors the main features of the CHERIoT hardware (including the newly introduced deep locality and deep immutability permissions). While our mini switcher doesn’t follow CHERIoT’s switcher instruction-by-instruction, it implements the same steps.

In this model, we proved on a range of small examples that the CHERIoT hardware-software co-design implements the expected memory-safety properties, and that the switcher’s overall design enforces both compartmentalisation and stack safety.

Our “end-to-end” results about concrete examples assume that the machine starts in a state that corresponds to the firmware image having been properly loaded. We have not verified the loader itself, and so it is part of our TCB. Technically, we consider executions only starting from a “loader-final” state. The loader is deterministic and so it is relatively easy to dump the contents of memory from a device (or simulator) after the loader has run and verify that a specific execution of the loader meets the properties required by our “loader-final” state.

We expect that it should be possible to prove the loader correct, but this is future work for now.

Our initial model was a simplification of CHERIoT: it didn’t support exceptions or concurrency/context switching, and some optimisations of the switcher (such as the stack high watermark) were left out.

According to recent reports, the CHERIoT team has been dedicated to making CHERIoT trustworthy, and has been very supportive of our verification effort. To that end, they included, in the switcher’s source, detailed comments about the expected invariants and behaviour of the switcher, in the form of pre- and post-conditions for the execution blocks. They pointed out that the complicated control flow in the switcher’s exception path was a likely source of errors.

In a recent development, our efforts highlighted that the cross-compartments call (and return) path that we verified was straightforward (although stating no-capture and stack safety at the separation logic level is not trivial!), but a good starting point. However, as pointed out by the CHERIoT team, the features that we initially left out are more prone to mistakes: the switcher’s exception handler (responsible for context switching and error handling) has a more fiddly and convoluted execution path, and the stack high watermark creates a upcoming point of trust.

By pursuing our verification effort to include the features missing from our initial model, some of the examples that we proved in the simplified setup did not work anymore, which actually uncovered bugs in the switcher.

The first bug that we uncovered comes from an interaction between the exception handler and the stack high watermark.

Industry observers note that in the presence of an exception handler, any instruction must either ensure that it cannot fault, or that the exception handler can safely execute (either by force-unwinding to the caller, or by giving control to the error handler of the faulting compartment). In our proof, this manifests as each instruction coming with a proof obligation that even when the instruction can fault, all invariants of the system are maintained.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, the stack high watermark (SHWM) is an optimisation allowing the switcher to clear only the stack frame used during the call. Specifically, the SHWM tracks, in hardware, the highest address of the stack that has been written to, and the switcher only clears up to this address, instead of the whole shared stack region. The code of the switcher relied on an invariant for the SHWM: it should always be in between the bounds of the stack capability at the point of a cross-compartment call. To that end, the switcher always re-sets it in the bounds of the stack capability at cross-compartment calls and returns. This invariant was very dynamic by nature, because the bounds of the stack change in between cross-compartment calls.

However, it turns out that this invariant did not hold: a malicious caller could craft a stack pointer with restricted bounds, together with a stack object outside of this restricted stack to be used later by a callee. This scenario can lead to a fault in the switcher return path of the callee, before it has cleared the callee stack frame, which then allows a malicious caller to recover the entire callee’s private state.

Industry observers note that we identified this problem when we tried to adapt our proof from a simplified switcher (without the SHWM), to a more faithful switcher (with the SHWM). The proof got stuck when we had to show that an adversary could not move the SHWM outside of the bounds of the stack. After a bit of investigation, we realised that it was not because we had failed to correctly capture the informal invariant, but because that invariant was not preserved. More specifically, it seemed to be possible for an attacker to move SHWM below the base of the stack capability.

We first tried to relax this (expected) invariant and allow SHWM to move below the base of the stack capability, but this condition was guarding a fault in the cross-compartment return-path. With the relaxed invariant, we had to prove that the fault was safe, which turned out to be impossible to prove, due to the callee’s stack frame being preserved. That’s how we realised that it was possible to mount an attack, with a subtle construction to move the SHWM below the base of the stack capability and exploiting the fault in the switcher’s return path to recover the uncleared callee’s stack frame.

The fix (merged in PR #799) ended up being pretty simple: by forbidding malicious callers from changing the base of the stack, it ensures that malicious callers cannot craft a stack object outside of the stack that would move the SHWM outside of the stack bounds. This does not prevent the caller from calling the callee with less than the maximum possible amount of stack space, but does require that the shared stack region is truncated in the same direction as normal stack allocation.

We could validate the fix in our setup, by completing the proof, before the merge.

According to recent reports, while verifying the context switching path in our simplified switcher, and in particular the path that an exited thread takes, we needed to define “what it means for a thread to exit”, and what is the authority that an exited thread still holds. We first looked at the scheduler’s code, in which exited threads are never meant to be scheduled anymore. Intuitively, we would think that an exited thread has no continuation.

However, the scheduler is not trusted for confidentiality or integrity (which are the properties we are verifying!), which means that in our model, we consider the scheduler as any other adversary compartment (and therefore, from our perspective, it contains arbitrary code). In particular, a malicious (or buggy) scheduler could schedule an exited thread, in which case the switcher re-instated that thread’s last context (as stored in the context switching save area), independently from whether that thread had exited. Because the thread exit path of the switcher never cleared the save area, an exited thread’s last context turned out to be whatever was left after the last preemption (or fault), which means that it could contain local capabilities that should not have been captured—clearly violating no-capture.

Industry observers note that we caught this bug because our formal verification method—focused on integrity and confidentiality—captures the threat model of CHERIoT, where the scheduler is no different from other adversaries with respect to those properties. The way the problem manifested in our proof is that we had to define what the authority of the continuation of an exited thread is, to account for what would happen if the thread were scheduled in a stale state. However, this looked fishy, and so we started questioning whether we should even have to consider such a situation.

Industry observers note that there are two disjoint sub-problems: (1) having access to an old register file (potentially breaking no-capture guarantees), and (2) an exited thread being re-scheduled. Sub-problem (1) is dangerous for integrity and confidentiality. Sub-problem (2) is a design question—what should happen if the scheduler reschedules an exited thread.

The fix (merged in PR #769) then fixed those problems: (1) the register file is cleared in the exit thread path (preventing an exited thread from using stale values) and (2) an exited thread becomes an idle thread looping in a wfi (wait-for-interrupt) loop. This fix was one of several possible fixes considered but was chosen because the scheduler always has the ability to run the idle thread (which loops in a wfi instruction). This meant that the ability to schedule an exited thread could be trivially shown to not increase the power of the scheduler.

With the fixed bugs, we have verified our Griotte switcher on top of our Griotte ISA, assuming that the loader initialises the machine properly.

That gave us confidence to scale our verification to be based on the whole authoritative cheriot-sail ISA, using the sail-to-rocq extraction, and our proofs of that are now complete. It means that we are quite confident that the current upstream switcher, together with the hardware, implement thread and compartments isolation, as well as no-capture.

In the future we would also like to verify the loader, and we also hope that our logical machinery can be used to verify correctness and security of applications running atop CHERIoT.

The focus of Cerise and Griotte has been advanced properties of capability machines, in particular involving non-monotonic domain transitions. As such, it is complementary to other formal verification work:.

Protecting data in memory from attackers continues to be a concern in computing systems. CHERI is a promising approach to achieve such protection, by providing and enforcing fine-grained memory protection directly in the hardware. Creating trust for the entire system stack, however, requires a gap-free verification of CHERI’s hardware-based protection mechanisms. Existing verification methods for CHERI target the abstract ISA model rather than the underlying hardware implementation. Fully ensuring the CHERI security guarantees for a concrete RTL implementation is a challenge in previous flows and demands high manual efforts. This paper presents VeriCHERI, a novel approach to security verification. It is conceptionally different from previous works in that it does not require any ISA specification. Instead of checking compliance with a golden ISA model, we check against well-established global security objectives of confidentiality and integrity. Fully covering these objectives, VeriCHERI uses as few as four unbounded properties to exhaustively prove or disprove any vulnerability. We demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of VeriCHERI on a RISC-V based processor implementing a CHERI variant.

Waypoint-1.5: Higher-Fidelity Interactive Worlds for Everyday GPUs

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (710 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.
  • Industry observers note that the first release of Waypoint demonstrated that real-time generative worlds were possible.
  • Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Waypoint-1.5 Weights on the Hub.

Waypoint-1.5 is Overworld’s next real-time video world model, built to bring interactive generative worlds to the hardware people actually own.

Industry observers note that the first release of Waypoint demonstrated that real-time generative worlds were possible. It proved that interactive world models could be more than passive video demos, and that locally runnable systems could begin to close the gap between generating a world and actually stepping into one.

Waypoint-1.5 builds directly on that foundation. This release improves visual fidelity, expands the range of hardware that can run the model locally, and takes another step toward interactive world simulation without datacenter-scale compute.

According to recent reports, on desktop hardware including RTX 3090 through 5090, Waypoint-1.5 can generate real-time environments at up to 720p and 60 FPS. This release also introduces a 360p tier designed to run smoothly across a much broader range of consumer hardware, including gaming laptops, and (soon) Apple Silicon Macs.

The biggest change in Waypoint-1.5 is accessibility.

With Waypoint-1, we proved the core experience. With Waypoint-1.5, we wanted to make that experience available on more machines without giving up real-time interactivity. That meant building two model tiers: a 720p model for higher-performance hardware, and a 360p model optimized for broader deployment.

Recent findings suggest that we also scaled training dramatically. Waypoint-1.5 was trained on nearly 100x more data than Waypoint-1, which significantly improves the model’s ability to generate more coherent environments and more consistent motion over time.

According to recent reports, under the hood, Waypoint-1.5 also incorporates more efficient video modeling techniques to reduce redundant computation across frames. That matters because real-time world models are not judged only by how a single frame looks. They are judged by whether the world responds instantly, stays coherent as you move through it, and remains usable on local hardware.

A lot of recent progress in generative video and world models has focused on visual fidelity. Those results matter, but fidelity alone is not what makes an interactive world feel real.

What people remember is responsiveness. They remember whether the environment reacts to them, whether motion stays coherent, whether the world holds together as they explore it, and whether the whole experience feels immediate instead of delayed.

That is the gap we care about most: the difference between watching a generated scene and actually being inside one.

If world models only run on large GPU clusters, they remain impressive demos. If they run locally on consumer hardware, they become something much more useful: a foundation for interactive entertainment, creative tooling, simulation, and AI-native environments people can actually explore.

Waypoint-1.5 is designed around that idea: not just better videos, but more responsive and explorable worlds that remain accessible on consumer hardware.

There are two ways to play Waypoint-1.5.

Industry observers note that the first is local execution through Overworld Biome. This release is designed to run across a wide range of hardware configurations, and the updated Biome runtime makes local setup much simpler. With the fresh installer flow, users can go from download to running the model locally in minutes.

The second is Overworld Stream, which lets you try Waypoint-1.5 instantly in the browser with no local setup required.

Whether you want immediate access or full local control, Waypoint-1.5 is built to support both.

Additionally, we provide World Engine, our flexible, easy to use, core inference library powering our official clients, along with nearly a dozen third party clients and libraries.

Waypoint started with a simple question: what would it take for generative worlds to become truly interactive?

Early generative systems highlighted that models could produce convincing images and videos. But building environments that people can explore, control, and interact with in real time is a different challenge entirely.

Waypoint-1.5 is another step in that direction, improving fidelity and expanding hardware accessibility while continuing to push real-time interactive generation onto local machines.

We think the future of world models will not be defined only by what they can render, but by whether people can actually inhabit and interact with them in real time.

Download Waypoint-1.5, run it locally with Biome, or jump in instantly on Overworld.stream.

And if you build something fun, strange, or unexpectedly immersive with it, we’d love to see it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, west Virginia's online casinos posted record monthly revenue in October 2026, the second full month with bet365 live in the state. The result pushed 2026 revenue past the total for all of 2025, while a bill to raise the iGaming tax remains pending.

It has been revealed that the revenue measure is adjusted gross interactive wagering receipts. State law defines it as an operator’s gross online wagering receipts minus winnings paid to players. Under 2019’s House Bill 2934, the privilege tax on those receipts goes into the Interactive Wagering Fund each week, and every licensed racetrack and historic resort pays it.

It has been revealed that bet365 released online sports betting and casino in the state on Aug. 27, 2026. West Virginia is its fourth U.S. online casino state. In its other 14 states, bet365 offers sports betting only.

Lottery licensing documents show bet365 received an interim license in January 2026. It was approved for a full annual license on July 29. West Virginia was the company’s sixth North American launch in 13 months, Yogonet reported. The earlier launches were Kansas and Maryland in August 2025, Missouri in December 2025, Michigan in April 2026 and Alberta in July 2026.

West Virginia’s market has a fixed structure. The Interactive Wagering Act allows no more than five gaming facility licenses with online wagering. Every online game counts as a state-owned lottery game. October’s record is consistent with bet365 adding to that market, but the operator split has yet to be shown.

Two months of 2026 remain to be reported. The comparison months set a high bar. Adjusted gross interactive gaming receipts were $37,198,210 in November 2025. Receipts for the fiscal year to date through Nov. 30, 2025, were $169,425,990.

It has been revealed that the broader lottery picture also shows growth. The Lottery took in more than $1.33 billion in gross revenue in fiscal 2026, which ended June 30. It sent $582.9 million to the state. Revenue was $58 million higher than in fiscal 2025. In its fiscal 2026 wrap-up, the Lottery named iLottery and iGaming as its biggest growth areas, and noted iGaming was following national gaming trends.

Higher revenue also raises the stakes of a pending tax change. Introduced on Jan. 16, 2026, House Bill 4397 would increase the iGaming privilege tax. The bill is still listed as pending in the House Local Governments Committee.

The next detail to watch is the operator breakdown. The Lottery publishes a file that splits interactive wagering data by skin and casino. That file will show how much of October’s record came from bet365.

Dutch data protection authority advises against purchasing AI camera glasses

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, advises consumers against purchasing AI camera glasses for general use.
  • Industry observers note that the AP had previously warned that filming bystanders is almost always prohibited.
  • It has been revealed that monique Verdier, Deputy Chair of the AP: “Glasses that film you without your knowledge are already a cause for concern.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), the Dutch data protection authority, advises consumers against purchasing AI camera glasses for general use. A study on six AI camera glasses, conducted by the AP itself, shows that these 'smart' glasses compromise not only the privacy of bystanders, but also the safety of consumers and those around them. For example, during a simulated resuscitation, one pair of glasses incorrectly indicated that an ambulance was on its way. Moreover, the glasses did not take sufficient account of the safety of minors, and the AP identified security problems in the software.

Industry observers note that the AP had previously warned that filming bystanders is almost always prohibited. The new study by the AP demonstrates that the risks extend beyond just privacy.

It has been revealed that monique Verdier, Deputy Chair of the AP: “Glasses that film you without your knowledge are already a cause for concern. Glasses that also give you the wrong advice when someone’s life is at stake go a step too far. AI offers many opportunities, provided that we are able to trust that technology. In the case of the camera glasses that we examined, that trust cannot be justified at present.”.

The AP investigated six AI camera glasses available on the Dutch market. Two of these were extensively tested in simulated real-life situations in which people’s safety was a key consideration.

According to recent reports, the results are alarming. During a simulated emergency in which advice on CPR was sought, one of the glasses claimed on several occasions that an ambulance was already on its way, even though no emergency services had been called. In a real emergency, such an error could result in essential help arriving too late, with potentially life-threatening consequences.

The AI camera glasses also made errors related to the protection of minors, with potentially very serious consequences. For example, one pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who was interested in a minor. In another test, safety warnings on toys for young children were not followed. The glasses also made mistakes when reading medicine leaflets and interpreting warnings about extreme weather.

The tests show that AI camera glasses can sound convincing, even if the information provided is incorrect or even dangerous. As a result, consumers may wrongly rely on advice that is not safe.

Sources indicate that in addition to these safety risks, the AP identified serious shortcomings in the protection of personal data. The recording lights on nearly all the camera glasses examined were barely visible and easy to cover up. Most glasses continued to film after the lights were covered, even though the manufacturer claimed this should not be possible. As a result, bystanders can hardly see whether they are being filmed.

Recent findings suggest that often, it is also unclear what happens to the footage and audio recordings. The AI functions examined process data through external servers, often located outside the European Union. Users are not provided with sufficient information about the AI models that process their data and the companies they share these data with. Furthermore, the AP discovered serious security complications with several pairs of glasses. As a result, someone nearby could connect to the glasses without permission, view recordings or even control the camera.

The AP at the moment considers AI camera glasses to be unsafe because of the risks they pose to owners and bystanders. The AP therefore advises consumers against buying AI camera glasses at this stage.However, the AP also recognises several legitimate uses for the technology. AI camera glasses can be valuable for people who are visually impaired or have low literacy levels, or who otherwise need support to understand their surroundings. But it is precisely for these users that it is crucial for the technology to be reliable.

The AP calls on developers of AI camera glasses to take more account of security, privacy and relevant legislation in the design and documentation of their products.

In a recent development, the AP calls on Dutch and European policymakers to include these fresh research findings in the further development of policies on AI camera glasses. “It is notable that we, as a society, learn to deal with these kinds of high-risk AI products. Simply banning everything provides some breathing space for now, but we cannot keep this up indefinitely. It is essential that we work collectively to raise awareness, build resilience and foster ethical consciousness,” claims Monique Verdier.

The AP recommends that owners and managers of locations prohibit the wearing and use of camera glasses in their house rules (in Dutch).

We built one of the most powerful computer-use AIs in the world. And made it directly accessible from your browser. On March 31st, we released Holo3, our most advanced computer-use model to date.

Recent findings suggest that building something powerful is one thing; making it accessible and easy to use is another. We’re doing both.

Industry observers note that holoTab is a Chrome extension that navigates the web just like a person would. It automates tasks across any website with zero setup or technical skills required. You describe what you want, and the agent handles it directly inside your browser, navigating interfaces, filling fields, and making decisions the same way you would. The vision models, the action planning, the interface understanding, all of it is running underneath, working for you, and all you ever see is the result.

Some tasks are quick and forgettable, but others are long and repetitive, the kind that reliably eat up your afternoon. You might find yourself cross-referencing competitor pricing across twenty different e-commerce tabs to update a master spreadsheet, or filtering through a dozen job boards and tech giant career pages to find new listings, painstakingly porting the details into a tracking doc to manage your applications.

Sources indicate that that's where routines come in. You start a recording, and HoloTab captures what you do in your tab in real time while you click or narrate along the way, demonstrating what you're doing and why. Your screen and your actions give HoloTab everything it needs, enriching the routine with enough context to actually understand the goal.

Once the recording stops, a routine is generated. From then on, you can re-run your routine or schedule it whenever you need to, and HoloTab will handle the rest on its own.

Computer-use AI is going to change how people work, research, and get things done, both in their professional and personal lives, and that shift is already closer than most people realize. But it shouldn't require a technical background to access, and the benefits shouldn't accrue only to teams with engineers who know how to wire these systems together.

HoloTab is free and ready for everyone to use today: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/holotab/hlaoiikljjgcjdhkakedfngifaopbcop.

#103626. Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2140 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Inside VAKRA: Reasoning, Tool Use, and Failure Modes of Agents

📅 15 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2140 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.
  • We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.
  • Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VAKRA Dataset | LeaderBoard | Release Blog | GitHub | Submit to Leaderboard.

We recently introduced VAKRA, a tool-grounded, executable benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents reason and act in enterprise-like environments.

Unlike traditional benchmarks that test isolated skills, VAKRA measures compositional reasoning across APIs and documents, using full execution traces to assess whether agents can reliably complete multi-step workflows.

Recent findings suggest that VAKRA provides an executable environment where agents interact with over 8,000+ locally hosted APIs backed by real databases spanning 62 domains, along with domain-aligned document collections. Tasks can require 3-7 step reasoning chains that combine structured API interaction with unstructured retrieval under natural-language tool-use constraints.

As can be seen below, models perform poorly on VAKRA - in this blog, we include additional dataset details about the tasks in VAKRA and present an analysis of failure modes we observed on different tasks.

As shown below, the VAKRA benchmark comprises of four tasks, each testing a different set of capabilities.

Fig 1: Representative examples of each capability in the VAKRA benchmark.

Industry observers note that this capability includes 2,077 test instances across 54 domains, requiring the use of tools from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD collections (Elder et al., 2026). Compared to the setup in Elder et al., the tool universe in SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD is expanded through the inclusion of a larger number of domains. Each domain is restricted to one tool collection, and tasks involve chaining 1–12 tool calls to arrive at the final answer.

Fig 2: Data sample from SEL-BIRD collection.

As shown above, each instance has an associated JSON data source from which the answer must be derived. The MCP servers supporting this task include a special tool, called get_data(tool_universe_id=id), which must be called at the beginning of each instance. This tool initializes the data source, returns a lightweight preview of the data (see below Figure 3), and stores the full dataset server-side to avoid large data transfers. This prevents the inefficient transfer of large data over the MCP protocol. The call also configures the MCP server to expose the appropriate tool set based on the tool_universe_id and aligns the data source with the domain-specific database for the instance.

The SLOT-BIRD collection provides a global set of 7 tools for generic data manipulation (e.g., filtering, sorting), inspired by systems like Tableau and Google Analytics. The SEL-BIRD collection extends this by introducing more specialized tools: some are shared with SLOT-BIRD, while others are derived by flattening categorical arguments into separate functions (e.g., sort_data with argument ascending: bool = False becomes sort_data_ascending and sort_data_descending). Additionally, the generic (retrieve_data) function from SLOT-BIRD is replaced with query-specific getters. Every key in the data for a given instance has an associated get function (get_KEY_NAME) for an average of 4 get functions per instance.

Fig 3: Data preview obtained from `get_data` function.

This capability includes 1,597 instances across 17 domains, requiring tools from an expanded REST-BIRD collection (Elder et al.). These use endpoint-style interfaces that provide highly specific, query-aligned endpoints that encapsulate most computation. They are served as REST APIs running in a FastAPI server, which is wrapped by the MCP server. This task requires selecting the correct APIs from the domain-specific tool set (as shown in the example in Figure 1). Each domain contains a minimum of 6 to a maximum of 328 tools (with an average of 116 tools). Similar to the previous task, the get_data tool configures the MCP server to expose only the relevant domain-specific APIs.

The OpenAI API Specification restricts the tool list input to a maximum length of 128 tools. This restriction requires an agent builder using this API to manage the length of the tool list directly via a shortlisting mechanism. In the baseline agents in our repository, a simple shortlisting capability handles this challenge.

The Capability 3 segment of the benchmark has 869 test instances drawn from 38 subject domains. These instances rely again on the REST-BIRD API collection, but add multi-hop reasoning to the challenge (refer to example in Figure 1). Multi-hop questions require multiple pieces of supporting evidence to be extracted and combined to reach an answer. The instances in this section require between one and five logical hops to answer a query. The question types distribution for queries within the test dataset is shown below in Figure 4.

Fig 4: API Hop-Type distribution for Capability 3 (MultiHop) and Hybrid Hop-Type distribution for Capability 4 (MultiHop MultiSource Reasoning).

Capability 4 includes 644 instances across 41 domains and is also built on the REST-BIRD API collection. Figure 4 above shows a distribution of hybrid hops for test queries without policies. It contains the most complex queries with the following characteristics:.

Multi-Source: This segment adds document indices per domain. Queries in this capability could require information from these document indexes as well as API calls. Similar to Capability 3, this task also has Multi-Hop queries. The required information source applies at the per-hop level, so, for example, a question may entail three logical hops with sources: API - RAG (Document Retrieval) - API. To enforce correct reasoning, sources are decontaminated during data generation, i.e. information required for a given hop is available in only one source. For example, if a hop is to be answered using APIs, the document index is built by removing documents that likely contain the information needed to answer the question.

Industry observers note that multi-Turn: This segment of the dataset also adds multi-turn conversations to the setting. Each instance is a dialog with multiple turns. The data is released as context-response pairs, where the context encodes the current dialog history and the agent is only responsible for answering the current turn.

Industry observers note that tool-usage Policies: A subset of these instances includes tool-use policies that the agent is required to follow. These policies take the form of plain-text instructions about the knowledge sources that the agent is allowed to access and under which circumstances. For example:.

In a recent development, the baseline agent in the project repo imposes adherence to these policies through a simple addition to the prompt: "You are a helpful assistant with access to tools.\n Tool Usage Constraint: {additional_instructions}.". Of course, agent builders are free to choose any constraint enforcement mechanism.

Recent findings suggest that VAKRA evaluates agents in tool environments where success depends on both the ability to execute coherent, multi-step workflows and answer correctness. We introduce an execution-centric evaluation framework that assesses not only final outputs but also the full tool-execution trajectory that includes tool calls, inputs, and intermediate results.

Industry observers note that the VAKRA Evaluator operates over two key inputs for each sample: a predicted final response and the corresponding tool-call trajectory. The tool calls from the predicted trajectory are executed in the same environment as the ground truth to verify intermediate tool outputs.

The evaluation follows a waterfall-style pipeline (Figure 6), where later stages are conditioned on earlier success:.

Fig 6: Waterfall-style Evaluation Pipeline.

Tool-Sequence Comparison Due to the presence of an executable environment, agents can explore the environment and sometimes return the answer by invoking a different set of APIs than the ones identified by us. In order to support alternative but valid tool invocations and reasoning paths, correctness is assessed by executing each predicted tool and comparing the set of tool responses against those from the ground truth (rather than enforcing strict step-level matching).

Specifically, we first perform a programmatic check, verifying whether all information present in the ground-truth tool responses is recovered by the predicted tool responses. This check may be inconclusive in cases involving partial matches, semantic equivalence, or differences in representation (e.g., ordering, aggregation, or formatting). In such cases, we apply a secondary LLM-based evaluation, adapted from the CRAG framework Yang et al., 2024, to determine whether the predicted trajectory retrieves all required information despite structural differences. This step uses an adapted prompt to determine whether the predicted trajectory captures all required information, even if obtained through a different sequence of tool calls.

According to recent reports, final Response Evaluation For trajectories that pass the previous check, the final response is evaluated using an LLM-based judge. This step ensures that the response is (i) grounded in the predicted tool outputs, and (ii) factually consistent with the ground truth answer, accounting for potential variations in phrasing or structure.

This design ensures that agents are rewarded not only for producing correct answers, but for obtaining them through valid and complete reasoning processes.

Every capability is equally weighted to obtain a final leaderboard score.

To obtain a capability score, every sample within a capability is equally weighted for capabilities 1 through 3.

For capability 4, we weight heterogeneous queries higher:.

Sources indicate that we now present detailed error analysis across the four VAKRA capabilities. To facilitate our analysis, we adopt stage-wise error categorization to assign each failure to the first point of breakdown. Specifically, we evaluate, in order: (i) whether the correct tool(s) were selected, (ii) whether the required arguments were provided without omissions or hallucinations, (iii) whether argument values were correct, and (iv) whether the final response is both accurate and grounded in the tool outputs.

Since a single sample may exhibit multiple errors across different steps, we sequentially classify each instance to the earliest failing stage (e.g., tool selection errors take precedence over argument errors). This avoids double-counting and allows error categories to be interpreted as disjoint fractions of the dataset. While more granular metrics (e.g., precision/recall over tool usage) are possible (Elder et al., 2026), we find this formulation provides a simple and interpretable breakdown of agent failures.

According to recent reports, the instances in this part of the benchmark required selecting and sequencing multiple tools to solve a single task. We have 2077 samples in this capability. This was challenging for all models, but GPT-OSS-120B performed best on this segment of the benchmark.

Fig 7: SEL-BIRD vs SLOT-BIRD Error Types Analysis.

The Business Intelligence (BI) API capability contains two sets of APIs, from the SLOT-BIRD and SEL-BIRD tool collections. The SEL part of this benchmark had 600 samples, while the SLOT part of the benchmark had 1477 samples. These two collections are grouped under the BI API capability, but have slightly different characteristics. The SLOT-BIRD collection has a smaller number of generic tools with a large number of parameter values to fill, while the SEL-BIRD collection has a larger set of tools and fewer parameters per tool. This focus is reflected in the relative errors made by models using these two tool collections.

Fig 8: Comparison of Accuracy Across Models by Hop Depth.

Multi-hop reasoning increases the difficulty of the original task by requiring models to successfully answer multiple implicitly coupled questions, each of which requires selecting and calling the correct API. As expected, all models performed best on the questions with only a single logical hop, and saw performance degradations on 2-hop and again on 3+ hop questions.

Fig 9: Model Accuracy Rates by Interaction Type (API, Document-Retriever, Hybrid).

Industry observers note that the final segment of the dataset includes document sources in addition to the tool/API sources in the other segments. This leads to instances that require single or multiple API calls, single or multiple document searches, or some combination of API calls and document searches.

Fig 10: Model Accuracy Rates by Policy Type.

According to recent reports, policies introduce an additional layer of difficulty on top of multi-hop, multi-source reasoning. When policies align with the required source for answering i.e. they do not affect the tool list required for models to answer the question, we refer to it as "No Updates to Answer" -- as shown in Figure 10, all models except for Granite-4.0-h-Small-32B experience a clear drop in performance under policy constraints that restrict access to the most relevant information source (i.e. "Policy updates the answer").

In general, we find that models either violate constraints or fail to retrieve sufficient information, where they sometimes understood the policy but could not answer the question correctly, or they exhibit one of the previously analyzed failure modes.

Overall, tool-use policy-constrained settings suggest that while models can reason over tools and sources, they struggle to incorporate external constraints into that reasoning - often a key requirement for reliable real-world deployment.

Sources indicate that VAKRA exposes a critical gap between surface-level tool competence and robust, end‑to‑end agent reliability. Although modern models can increasingly select APIs and execute isolated tool calls, VAKRA indicates that these abilities alone are insufficient for real‑world deployment. In practice, models often break down when required to perform compositional reasoning under execution constraints—spanning APIs, documents, dialog context, and policy requirements.

Run it on VAKRA and see where it falls apart—tool selection, multi-hop reasoning, or policy constraints.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Michigan's regulator has approved the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe's move of its Soaring Eagle online casino and sportsbook from GAN to White Hat Gaming.
  • According to recent reports, soaring Eagle Gaming has a new technology partner in Michigan.
  • Platform swaps like this are rare in Michigan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michigan's regulator has approved the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe's move of its Soaring Eagle online casino and sportsbook from GAN to White Hat Gaming. The rare platform swap gives White Hat a full platform role in a top-three US market while GAN's owner restructures the business.

According to recent reports, soaring Eagle Gaming has a new technology partner in Michigan. The Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe’s online casino and online sports betting operations now run on White Hat Gaming Inc.’s platform. White Hat replaces GAN, which had powered the tribe’s Michigan offer since launch. That launch came under the Eagle Casino and Sports brand.

Platform swaps like this are rare in Michigan. Players keep the same Soaring Eagle brand.

The board reviewed the White Hat platform and the tribe’s branding submission before signing off. The tribe also filed a signed agreement with White Hat. Every supplier and vendor needed for launch had already been approved. Executive Director Henry Williams said the board checked the new platform carefully against its standards on integrity, security and consumer protection, which apply to any platform Michigan players use.

The approval carries conditions. Both companies are limited to games, sports events and bet types the board has approved, and must route business through approved suppliers, vendors and payment locations. Both companies must also fully adopt all internal control amendments the board has approved.

The board’s list of authorized platform providers now names White Hat as the tribe’s provider for online casino and online sports betting. The tribe already had a content tie to White Hat Studios, the games supplier. In June 2022, White Hat Studios confirmed it would supply branded games, including Ted, Deal or No Deal and Peaky Blinders, to the tribe’s PlayEagle.com site.

The stakes in Michigan remain sizable. Operators reported $355.7 million in combined online casino and online sports betting gross receipts for September 2026, up 5.4% from August. Online casino accounted for $300.2 million and sports betting for $55.5 million. Adjusted gross receipts came to $313.04 million. Online casino adjusted receipts, however, fell 0.9% from August. The figures are consistent with a market still growing year on year but flatter month to month.

It has been revealed that the switch comes as GAN works through changes under newly introduced ownership. In results for the six months to September 30, 2026, Sega Sammy said GAN is running a turnaround program that cuts fixed costs. The program will also move GAN ahead with migrating to a new platform. Adding GAN and Stakelogic raised group sales. It also widened the operating loss compared with the same period a year earlier.

According to recent reports, november 9-13 is Illegal Gambling Awareness Week. We're proud to partner with International Association of Gaming Regulators (IAGR) to raise awareness about the risks of illegal gambling. Regulation helps protect players. Illegal operators intentionally operate outside the law,… pic.twitter.com/WhKHVIdVZJ.

— Michigan Gaming Control Board (@MichiganGCB) November 9, 2026.

According to recent reports, white Hat’s own structure is shifting too. Merkur Group agreed in July 2026 to buy the content supplier White Hat Studios for an undisclosed sum. The White Hat Gaming platform and white-label businesses are not part of that deal. They stay with their current owners. The Merkur purchase of White Hat Studios remains pending regulatory approval.

It has been revealed that this post will describe an algorithm for constructing an ANF/similar IR from a functional-like base language with no closure usage, and with no related excess space requirements. This algorithm is as far as I know not new, and has apparently been known in imperative compilation for a while. However, I admittedly have no source for this, nor have I seen it described for functional-like languages.

Thanks to Ryan Brewer and rpjohnst for their inspiration on this.

If you are only interested in code, please skip to Implementation.

It has been revealed that first, let us describe our input and output languages. Our input language will look like this:.

This is meant to echo some simple functional programming language, and contains all the elements needed to demonstrate the algorithm.

Our output language will look like a lexically-scoped flat ANF-style construction, with all lets at the toplevel. The goal is to convert from our input ml to this language.

The notable addition is the Hole constructor in anf, the purpose of which will be described now.

Imagine we are trying to convert the term.

According to recent reports, when we arrive at the body of x, we have a conundrum. We need to put the conversion of y before x, so that using y is well-scoped. Hence, we must convert y before we can continue. How do we use this conversion, though? x's content needs to be put in the anf field of y's Let, so it's not clear how to both convert y before x and to use x's finished conversion in y.

One "traditional" method of solving this is via continuations, where y is passed a closure representing "what to do next", after it converts its body. We can then put x's content in that closure, which will be invoked later. This has two main flaws:.

Industry observers note that recall that we left a Hole of anf option ref field in our anf type. I will denote a hole like this: [·]. The central idea is that our conversion of any given ml fragment will return:.

Consider this simplified example:.

Sources indicate that when we convert x, this signals for the conversion of y. There are two steps to converting a let - we must first convert the "head" (2), and then the "body" (y).

Converting the head will result in something of form.

Recent findings suggest that note that the hole is left to be filled later. This way, the conversion of y's head need know nothing about its environment. We represent this in code via the Hole constructor, which contains a reference to a fragment that either may be empty (None) or filled (Some ...). The conversion of the body can then proceed by first generating the expected addition, binding it to nm so it may be referenced later:.

Industry observers note that we now need to get this fragment into the proper lexical scope. We can do this by plugging it into the hole left by the conversion of the head:.

Then, returning this fragment, the name bound (y), and the reference to the inner hole, we can continue converting x; First, convert the head, using the name returned by the conversion of y:.

And finally plug it into the hole returned by y.

We are left with a final hole we can plug with Done to be explicit about the end of a control flow path. One disadvantage of this strategy is that it does generate many unneeded names. Most of these can be avoided by carefully special casing certain lets, and the rest can be eliminated via a simple folding pass.

Below is a sample implementation of this algorithm, in OCaml.

Industry observers note that I recommend toying with the conversion yourself, using utop or similar. In the following, I will "clean up" the output slightly, as to not make it unreadable.

If we use our first example term:.

We can then plug the returned hole, as described. Via some inspection, we can verify this is indeed correct, and conforms to our ANF-like form, as expected.

As mentioned earlier, the large amount of duplicate names can be mitigated through strategies such as special casing let _ = and folding passes.

Clearly, the algorithm does not use closures, or any indirect jumps. It does not allocate any more than needed for the representation of the output program; there is no excessive closure allocation. I do not presently have a good way to test performance on real-world large inputs, but I have no reason to believe it would not perform better than an equivalent higher-order version.

I believe this method should be extendable to CPS as well, although I have not tried as of the moment. The "usual" higher-order CPS conversion described in e.g. "Compiling with continuations, continued" looks quite similar to the higher-order presentation of ANF conversion, so I would be interested in whether it can be similarly massaged into a mutable form.

Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 16 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Industry observers note that as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query.
  • Industry observers note that if you're fresh to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. In my previous blogpost, I introduced the newly introduced multimodal capabilities, showing how to use embedding and reranker models that handle text, images, audio, and video. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to train or finetune these multimodal models on your own data.

Industry observers note that as a practical example, I'll walk through finetuning Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for Visual Document Retrieval (VDR), the task of retrieving relevant document pages (as images, with charts, tables, and layout intact) for a given text query. The resulting tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr demonstrates how much performance you can gain by finetuning on your own domain. On my evaluation data, the finetuned model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 compared to the base model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models I tested against, including models up to 4x its size.

Industry observers note that if you're fresh to multimodal models in Sentence Transformers, I recommend reading Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers first. For training text-only embedding, reranker, or sparse embedding models, see the Prior Blogposts section at the end.

General-purpose multimodal embedding models like Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B are trained on diverse data to perform well across a wide range of languages and tasks: image-text matching, visual question answering, document understanding, and more. But this generality means the model is rarely the best choice for any specific task.

It has been revealed that consider Visual Document Retrieval: given a text query like "What was the tech giant's Q3 revenue?", the model must find the most relevant document screenshot from a corpus of thousands. This requires understanding document layouts, charts, tables, and text, which is a very different skill from e.g. matching pictures of shoes with product descriptions.

By finetuning on domain-specific data, the model can learn these specialized patterns. In my experiment, finetuning improved NDCG@10 from 0.888 to 0.947, ahead of every recent multimodal model I tested, including ones up to 4x larger.

Training multimodal Sentence Transformer models involves the same components as training text-only models:.

The multimodal training pipeline uses the same SentenceTransformerTrainer as text-only training. The key difference is that your datasets contain images (or other modalities) alongside text, and the model's processor handles the image preprocessing automatically.

Let's walk through each component, using Visual Document Retrieval (matching text queries to document screenshots) as a running example.

In a recent development, the most common approach is to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model, or to start from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) checkpoint. The Transformer module automatically detects supported modalities from the model's processor.

In a recent development, to finetune an existing multimodal embedding model (e.g. one that already has a modules.json file), you can pass processor_kwargs and model_kwargs to control preprocessing and model loading respectively. processor_kwargs are passed directly to AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(...) (e.g., image resolution bounds: higher max_pixels means higher quality but more memory), while model_kwargs are passed to the appropriate AutoModel.from_pretrained(...) call (e.g., precision, attention implementation):.

Industry observers note that you can also start from a fresh VLM checkpoint that hasn't been trained for embeddings yet. Sentence Transformers will attempt to recognize the architecture, infer the supported modalities from the processor, and set up the appropriate forward method and pooling. If the automatic detection doesn't work perfectly for a particular model, the configuration in the saved sentence_bert_config.json can be edited to adjust modality settings, forward methods, and output handling:.

Sources indicate that in both cases, the Transformer module inspects the processor to determine which modalities are available, and Pooling is added automatically if needed. You can verify the supported modalities:.

Instead of using a single VLM backbone, you can compose separate encoders for different modalities using the Router module. This lets you combine any existing encoders and route inputs to the appropriate one based on detected modality:.

Recent findings suggest that since Router-based multimodal models use separate encoders per modality, their embedding spaces are initially unaligned. Training is required to align the spaces for meaningful cross-modal similarity. The Dense projection layer shown above helps map embeddings from different encoders into a shared space.

It has been revealed that this approach is useful when you want to use lightweight, specialized encoders rather than a large VLM. You can also combine Router-based multimodality with task-based routing (e.g. different encoders for queries vs. documents) using route_mappings. See the Router documentation for advanced routing scenarios.

In a recent development, for this example, I use the tomaarsen/llamaindex-vdr-en-train-preprocessed dataset, a preprocessed English subset of llamaindex/vdr-multilingual-train. The source dataset was released alongside the Visual Document Retrieval Goes Multilingual blogpost by LlamaIndex, and consists of ~500k multilingual query-image samples collected from public internet PDFs, with queries synthetically generated using VLMs (gemini-1.5-pro and Qwen2-VL-72B). My preprocessed version filters to the 53,512 English samples and resolves 4 of the 16 ID-based hard negatives per sample into actual document screenshot images, so it can be used directly for training without further preprocessing:.

Sources indicate that the train config contains the first 10,000 samples, and the eval config contains the next 300 samples (a full config with all 53,512 samples is also available). For training, I select query, image, and negative_0 to form (anchor, positive, hard negative) triplets. Including additional hard negatives would likely improve the training signal, but each extra negative also increases memory usage and training time, so I stick with one. For evaluation, I keep all four hard negatives per query to build a more challenging retrieval corpus (more on that in the Evaluator section).

Just like text-only training, the dataset format must match your chosen loss function. The rules are the same:.

For multimodal datasets, the inputs can contain:.

Sources indicate that the data collator automatically calls model.preprocess(), which detects the modality of each input and applies the appropriate preprocessing. No manual tokenization or image processing is needed.

Many Hugging Face datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers, allowing you to easily find them at https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers.

Industry observers note that for this training, I use CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, a common choice for retrieval tasks. It accepts (query, positive) pairs with any number of additional hard negative columns, from 0 up to n, as long as each sample has the same number of negatives. During training, the loss pushes each query's similarity to its positive up and its similarity to every negative down. The negatives come from two sources:.

More negatives per query means a stronger training signal, so a larger batch size directly improves training quality. Beyond that, the "cached" variant of the loss uses gradient caching to make large effective batch sizes feasible even when GPU memory is limited.

It has been revealed that the mini_batch_size parameter controls how many samples are processed at once during the cached forward passes. For large multimodal models, setting this to a small value (e.g., 1) is important to avoid out-of-memory errors without sacrificing the benefits of large effective batch sizes:.

Industry observers note that to produce embeddings that work well at multiple dimensionalities, I wrap the base loss with MatryoshkaLoss. This trains the model so that truncating the embedding to a smaller number of dimensions still yields good performance:.

In a recent development, this is especially useful for multimodal models, where embeddings can be large (2048 dimensions for Qwen3-VL). With Matryoshka training, you can use truncated embeddings (e.g., 256 or 128 dimensions) at deployment time for faster search with minimal quality loss. As I'll show in the Results section, the finetuned model achieves near-peak performance even at 512 dimensions.

The SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments class lets you control training hyperparameters. Here's the configuration used for the VDR finetuning:.

A few things to note for (multimodal) training:.

To track retrieval performance before, during, and after training, I use the InformationRetrievalEvaluator. It computes standard retrieval metrics like NDCG@10, MAP, and Recall@k:.

Industry observers note that the evaluator takes text queries, a corpus of images (including hard negatives), and a mapping of which documents are relevant to which queries. Note that the corpus contains a mix of positive and hard negative document screenshots, making this a challenging evaluation. Using batch_size=1 prevents out-of-memory complications during evaluation of the large VLM.

The SentenceTransformerTrainer brings everything together. Here's the complete training script:.

In a recent development, the training script is nearly identical to a text-only training script. The only differences are:.

Everything else (the trainer, training arguments, dataset loading) works exactly the same as text-only training.

In a recent development, after training for just 1 epoch, the finetuned tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr model achieves an NDCG@10 of 0.947 on the evaluation set (300 queries, 1500 corpus documents, cosine similarity). This is a significant improvement over the base Qwen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B model's 0.888, and outperforms all existing VDR models:.

It has been revealed that the finetuned 2B model outperforms even the 8B Qwen3-VL-Embedding model, demonstrating the power of task-specific finetuning. Finetuning on your own domain is often worth considering, even when a larger general-purpose model is available!

Industry observers note that the comparison above uses full-size 2048-dim embeddings. Thanks to the Matryoshka training, the finetuned model also holds up well when truncated to fewer dimensions, letting you trade off embedding size and retrieval quality at deployment time:.

The finetuned model's peak is at the full 2048 dimensions (0.948), but it stays within 0.3% of peak all the way down to 512 (4x smaller), and retains over 92% of peak even at 64 (32x smaller). Matryoshka training concentrates the most important information in the earlier dimensions, so moderate truncation costs very little performance.

According to recent reports, the gap between 1024 and 2048 dimensions is small (0.946 vs. 0.948), so I've saved the model with truncate_dim=1024 set in its configuration. This means that SentenceTransformer("tomaarsen/Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B-vdr") produces 1024-dimensional embeddings by default, halving the storage footprint compared to the full 2048. If you want a different dimensionality, pass truncate_dim=N when loading to override it.

You can also finetune multimodal Cross Encoder (reranker) models using the same training infrastructure. The key difference is using CrossEncoderTrainer and Cross Encoder-specific loss functions. This section provides a brief overview; see the full training examples for complete, runnable scripts with dataset preparation and evaluation.

Here's a simplified example based on the doodles training script, which trains a reranker to match images with text captions:.

There are multiple valid architectural choices for multimodal rerankers, including:.

Both approaches are demonstrated in the multimodal cross encoder training examples.

The two scripts linked above split the training data into two datasets, one per direction (image-to-text and text-to-image), with a task-specific prompt for each that tells the model how to score in that direction. Each positive pair is then expanded with randomly sampled negatives so the loss sees a balanced mix of matches and non-matches.
