💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI released Privacy Filter on the Hub this week: an open-source personally-identifiable information (PII) detector that labels text across eight categories in a single forward pass over a 128k context.
  • All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK.
  • Privacy Filter is a 1.5B-parameter model with 50M active parameters, permissively licensed under Apache 2.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI released Privacy Filter on the Hub this week: an open-source personally-identifiable information (PII) detector that labels text across eight categories in a single forward pass over a 128k context. Model card. We spent a few hours building with it and landed on three apps that each reveals a different slice of what it can do.

All three are built on gradio.Server, which lets you pair custom HTML/JS frontends with Gradio's queueing, ZeroGPU allocation, and gradio_client SDK. In all these apps, gradio.Server plays the same backend role, and that consistency is exactly what makes it really powerful.

Privacy Filter is a 1.5B-parameter model with 50M active parameters, permissively licensed under Apache 2.0. PII categories are private_person, private_address, private_email, private_phone, private_url, private_date, account_number, secret. Context is 128,000 tokens. Achieves state-of-the-art performance on the PII-Masking-300k benchmark. Full numbers and methodology are in the official release blog.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Document-PII-Explorer.

Sources indicate that user problem. You want to read a PII-heavy document (a contract, a resume, an exported chat log) with every detected span highlighted by category, a filter in the sidebar, and a summary dashboard up top. The reading experience should feel like a normal document, not a form.

Sources indicate that what Privacy Filter does here. The whole file goes through in a single 128k-context forward pass, so there's no chunking, no stitching, and span offsets line up directly with the rendered text. BIOES decoding keeps span boundaries clean through long ambiguous runs.

What gr.Server does here. You could wire this up in Blocks with gr.HighlightedText and a sidebar, and it would work. The reading experience we wanted (serif body, category filters that toggle CSS classes client-side instead of re-running the model, a summary dashboard that doesn't force a page re-render) was easier to hand-author than to compose. gr.Server lets us serve the reader view as a single HTML file and expose the model behind one queued endpoint:.

Note the decorator: @server.api(name="analyze_document"), not a plain @server.post. That's the piece that plugs the handler into Gradio's queue, so concurrent uploads are serialized, @spaces.GPU composes correctly on ZeroGPU, and the same endpoint is reachable from both the browser and gradio_client with no duplicated code. The browser calls it with the Gradio JS client:.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-Image-Anonymizer.

User problem. You want to share an image or any screenshot (a Slack thread, a receipt, a Stripe dashboard) with black bars over the PII. You want to toggle bars on and off, drag them to reposition, or draw one by hand for anything the model missed, then export the result.

What Privacy Filter does here. Tesseract runs OCR and returns per-word bounding boxes. The backend reconstructs the full text with a char-offset to box map, then runs Privacy Filter once over the whole text. Detected character spans are looked up against the word map and joined into pixel rectangles per line.

According to recent reports, what gr.Server does here. gr.ImageEditor supports layered annotation and is a reasonable starting point for image redaction. The workflow we wanted (per-bar category metadata, toggle all bars in a category at once, client-side PNG export at natural resolution with no server round-trip) was cleaner to build on a custom frontend. gr.Server hands back pixel rectangles from one queued endpoint and lets the canvas own everything else:.

In a recent development, the frontend invokes it with client.predict("/anonymize_screenshot", { image: handle_file(file) }), the same pattern as above. Toggles, drags, fresh-bar drawing, and PNG export all happen in the browser; edits never round-trip to the server.

Try it at ysharma/OPF-SmartRedact-Paste.

In a recent development, user problem. You want a pastebin that redacts before sharing. You paste a log line, an email, a support ticket. You get two URLs back. The public one serves the redacted version with , , placeholders, following the redaction convention from the official blog examples. The private one is gated by a token you keep and shows the original with spans highlighted.

Recent findings suggest that what Privacy Filter does here. Swap each detected span with a placeholder on the stored paste. That's the entire redaction step. Multilingual text (Spanish, French, Chinese, Hindi, and others in the model-card examples) routes through the same call with no change.

What gr.Server does here. This app needs two distinct GET routes for the same paste ID, one public and one token-gated, and the URL shape matters because the reveal URL is the thing you keep. gr.Server works here because it's a FastAPI app underneath — which is also why @server.api and plain @server.get can sit side by side in the same process. Note: this can also be built with gr.Blocks() by mounting custom routes with FastAPI :.

In a recent development, A daemon thread evicts expired pastes every 30 seconds. The whole service, including storage, is about 200 lines of application code because everything lives in one process.

The split across all three apps is the same — anything that touches the model goes through @server.api, everything else stays on plain FastAPI routes:.

@server.api gives you Gradio's queue (serialized requests, correct @spaces.GPU composition on ZeroGPU, progress events) and it's what the browser hits through @gradio/client. The same endpoint is also what gradio_client users hit from Python — one function, two SDKs, no duplicated code. Plain @server.get/@server.post are reserved for the static surfaces: HTML pages, file lookups, cheap dict reads. That's the rule of thumb from the gradio.Server intro post, and it's what makes these three apps feel consistent even though their UIs are very different.

It has been revealed that drop in a resume, a screenshot of a Slack thread, a log line with a token in it. The fun part is seeing what Privacy Filter catches (and occasionally misses) on text you actually care about.

Nice demos — the 8-category Privacy Filter taxonomy is a strong EN consumer/sanitization baseline for pastebins and screenshots.

Sources indicate that one gap I keep hitting for clinical notes outside EN: taxonomy coverage ≠ “run the same 8 labels on another language/domain.” Locale clinical text needs entity classes and distractors that the EN consumer schema doesn’t encode; otherwise you measure a different product than the one you deploy. Synthetic labeled notes help for that coverage test before anyone claims compliance.

Curious whether you’ve tried feeding clinical-style notes (even synthetic) through the same 8 labels and where the misses concentrate.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different company” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a massive difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company.

Clarke said he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

Industry observers note that dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

Recent findings suggest that HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the organization’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO stated HPE expects better growth ahead, because fresh server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

In a recent development, dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News QCon San Francisco 2026: Automating Spark Upgrades with Codex Agents at OpenAI.

Nov 25, 2026 2 min read.

It has been revealed that at QCon San Francisco 2026, Mouli Mukherjee, Engineering Manager for Data Infrastructure at OpenAI, argued that AI agents are most useful not for rebuilding a data platform, but for the open-ended operational work that is hard to turn into fixed playbooks. OpenAI’s platform runs at exabyte scale, with hundreds of thousands of datasets and a Spark fleet on millions of cores, and Mukherjee showed how Codex-driven agents can take on that kind of work when the right systems sit underneath them.

In a recent development, mukherjee clearly distinguished between deterministic systems and agents. She stated that anything requiring consistent outputs for the same inputs, such as access control, configuration resolution, and data correctness guarantees, should remain within the realm of proper systems. Agents utilize these systems as tools and do not attempt to reimplement them. As she expressed:.

We should definitely build the systems where we want guarantees and guardrails.

Agents earn their place where failure modes and remediations cannot be fully enumerated in advance, such as debugging: follow the evidence, decide what to try next, and stay inside the tools’ guarantees.

The Spark upgrade outlines steps taken to ensure safety. The team first built a shadow-run service for testing, which reused production inputs and operated on a low-priority queue to avoid impacting live operations. They also implemented a configuration override service to prevent experiments from changing global settings and developed a validation skill to compare production and shadow runs. After these safeguards were in place, agents claimed jobs, debuted shadow runs, reviewed validation reports, classified errors, and transitioned jobs to the newly introduced Spark version.

Mukherjee reported that the same primitives now cover more of routine platform operations. Agents can tune job efficiency continuously by inspecting query plans, trying a config change, comparing runs, and iterating. For lower-risk incremental library releases, the team sometimes skips the shadow step and promotes directly, trading capacity for higher rollback risk. Jobs that pass shadow validation but later fail in production can auto-roll back to the previous Spark version so pipelines keep running without manual intervention. On the support side, agents can search past incident reports, suggest runbook updates, trace why a table is stale through orchestrator and scheduler logs, and help consumers understand access-control denials, while permissions still enforce the user’s own credentials.

Mukherjee recommended starting with the repetitive, open-ended tasks where judgment matters and failure modes are too numerous to hard-code, building the safety mechanisms first, and only then letting agents operate inside those bounds so experimentation stays repeatable, observable, and reversible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benchmark highlightsBuilding on Nemotron Nano V2 VL, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers substantial visual gains and adds entirely newly introduced audio and video+audio capabilities - while also leading another open-weights omni model, Qwen3-Omni, in many domains.

According to recent reports, efficiency highlightsCompared to other open omni models with the same interactivity, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni delivers 7.4x higher system efficiency for multi-document use cases and 9.2x higher system efficiency for video use cases Figure 1. Total system throughput for multi-document and video use cases sustained by each model at a fixed per‑user interactivity threshold (tokens/sec/user).

At a high level, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is aimed at five classes of workloads:.

In a recent development, this is not only about OCR. The model is positioned for long, messy, high-value documents where understanding depends on layout, tables, figures, formulas, section structure, and cross-page references. Think contracts, technical papers, reports, manuals, multi-page forms, or compliance packets. The model can handle 100+ page documents.

According to recent reports, nemotron 3 Nano Omni includes strong speech understanding capabilities that enable high-quality transcription across diverse audio conditions. It handles long-form audio with varying speakers, accents, and background noise. These capabilities can be integrated into broader workflows, allowing spoken content to be transcribed, analyzed, and combined with other modalities for tasks like summarization, question answering, and cross-modal reasoning.

Recent findings suggest that many enterprise and developer workflows depend on mixed audio and visual evidence: screen recordings with narration, training videos, meetings with slides, tutorials, product demos, customer support captures, and long-form video archives. Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is built to reason over those inputs jointly.

Recent findings suggest that the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model is specifically trained for agentic computer use, enabling it to assist with tasks in graphical user interface (GUI) environments. Its capabilities include interpreting screenshots, monitoring the state of the user interface, grounding its reasoning in on-screen visuals, and helping with action selection or workflow automation.

The model is designed for more than perception. It excels at reasoning-intensive tasks that require synthesizing information across long context windows, multiple modalities, and structured or semi-structured evidence. It can carry out multi-step reasoning, perform calculations, and connect signals from text, images, tables, and other inputs to arrive at coherent, well-supported answers.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a unified encoder-projector-decoder design. The language backbone is Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B, paired with the C-RADIOv4-H vision encoder and the Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2 audio encoder. The modality-specific encoders connect into the LLM backbone through lightweight projectors.

It has been revealed that figure 2. Model architecture of NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni 30B-A3B.

The model backbone interleaves three key components: 23 Mamba selective state-space layers for efficient long-context processing; 23 MoE layers with 128 experts, top-6 routing, and a shared expert for conditional capacity; and 6 grouped-query attention layers to preserve strong global interaction and expressivity.

Nemotron 3 Nano Omni combines state-space models, attention, and MoE in a unified design that maintains strong reasoning performance while remaining practical for long, multimodal contexts.

In a recent development, on the vision side, the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni replaces the tiling strategy used in the v2 model with dynamic resolution processing at native aspect ratio. Each image can be represented using a variable number of 16 x 16 patches, with a minimum of 1,024 to a maximum of 13,312 visual patches per image. For square images, this is equivalent to 512 x 512 and 1840 x 1840, respectively.

That flexibility is critical for handling high-resolution, complex visual inputs such as OCR-heavy documents, financial tables, slides, research figures, screenshots, and GUI layouts—especially when both fine details and overall structure need to be understood together.

In a recent development, for video, Nemotron 3 Nano Omni uses a dedicated Conv3D tubelet embedding path. Instead of embedding each frame independently, every pair of consecutive frames is fused into a single "tubelet" before the ViT, halving the number of vision tokens the language model has to attend to. This allows us to either double the number of frames with the same token budget, or halve the number of tokens with the same number of frames.

EVS is an important feature, enabled during inference time, that drops redundant video tokens after the vision encoder. This reduces latency and improves throughput while maintaining accuracy. The first frame of the video is kept entirely, then for each subsequent frame, EVS keeps the “dynamic” tokens where the video is changing and drops the “static” ones where nothing has changed from the previous frame. We combine this with Conv3D to enable superior compression: Conv3D fuses tokens from pairs of frames into one, and then EVS prunes redundant static information.

According to recent reports, the audio side is powered by Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v2, connected to the backbone through its own 2-layer MLP projector. Audio is sampled at 16 kHz, and the model is trained with inputs up to 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), while the LLM max context length supports 5+ hours.

It has been revealed that this represents a shift from traditional VLM pipelines by enabling native audio processing within a shared multimodal sequence, allowing audio, visual, and text tokens to be jointly modeled. This is crucial for scenarios like narrated screen recordings, video Q&A where speech alters visual meaning, long-form instructional or meeting content, and tasks requiring temporally grounded multimodal reasoning.

It has been revealed that each encoder is connected to the LLM with a lightweight 2-layer MLP projector that maps encoder features into the shared embedding space. Once projected, vision, audio, and text tokens are interleaved and processed jointly.

This design keeps the overall system modular while still enabling genuine cross-modal reasoning inside the backbone itself.

The SFT stages are trained on NVIDIA H100, scaling from 32 to 128 nodes depending on the stage. The stack uses Megatron-LM, Transformer Engine, and Megatron Energon, with tensor parallelism, expert parallelism, sequence parallelism, context parallelism for the long context stages, online sequence packing, and selective activation recomputation.

Sources indicate that post-SFT reinforcement learning uses NeMo-RL and NeMo Gym with a Megatron backend. The RL infrastructure used a Ray-based distributed setup across B200 and H100 clusters, plus multimodal deduplication, so repeated rollouts do not multiply image, video, and audio memory.

We open-source substantial parts of our training code.

We introduce multi-environment text and omni training in Nemotron 3 Nano Omni. Our text RL training stage happens across diverse environments in Nemo-Gym, which evaluates the model’s ability to perform sequences of actions such as tool calling, writing code, and multi-part planning that satisfy the verifiable criteria.

Omni RL trains the model to reason across images, video, audio, and text within a unified framework, covering tasks from single-modality to fully multimodal scenarios. A diverse verifier suite evaluates outputs across formats like multiple-choice, math, GUI grounding, and ASR, while intentionally including unanswerable cases to teach the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient rather than hallucinate.

Industry observers note that nemotron 3 Nano Omni is trained on an enhanced dataset that emphasizes high-quality reasoning across multiple modalities. We significantly expand task coverage and introduce synthetic data for complex reasoning scenarios where public datasets are limited. To support this, we build task-specific, multi-stage pipelines for scalable synthetic data generation.

Industry observers note that as one example, we generated approximately 11.4M synthetic QA pairs (~45B tokens) from a large corpus of real-world PDFs using NeMo Data Designer. This dataset is used to strengthen long-context document reasoning during post-training and delivers a 2.19× improvement in overall accuracy on MMLongBench-Doc.

We detail the full pipeline evolution, including failure analysis and key lessons learned, in our Data Designer developer note. The note also includes nine runnable pipeline recipes that can serve as starting points for building your own document-understanding datasets.

Sources indicate that nemotron 3 Nano Omni can analyze and reason over long documents such as financial reports, academic papers, product manuals, etc. The following example retrieves financial metrics across a 100+ page document to calculate another metric:.

Figure 3: Stylized example from the MMLongBench-Doc benchmark.

The model was prompted to answer the question as follows:.

The model is capable of long-context retrieval, structured extraction, table/chart reading and multi-page reasoning all in one go.

Sources indicate that nemotron-3 Nano Omni performs joint audio-visual analysis, both locally for specific scenes and globally across the entire video. #103603. Abolish Lock Poisoning

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1376 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pocoo ↗ Open Full Page

Abolish Lock Poisoning

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1376 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pocoo

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning.
  • Sources indicate that personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me.
  • In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex, the mutex is poisoned. That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError. The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state.

Sources indicate that personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.

In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.

Industry observers note that primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning.

Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.”.

When a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all.

Industry observers note that that’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only matter with the system today. So here I want to share some of the concerns and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten.

One subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock!

Recent findings suggest that that can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives (#159930).

This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server.

Deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless:.

In a recent development, while not live services, test suites show the same general matter. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError. This problem demonstrated up for cargo, deno, polars and rustc itself.

If you recover with into_inner(), the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:.

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

Recent findings suggest that so who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015, two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Same with the panic output capture, the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock. They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison.

Industry observers note that and I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison. When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing.” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell. Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

In a recent development, take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell, and you have exactly the same problem. Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError, the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the issue.

Given how much panic catching goes on in async code, much of which is !Send for performance reasons, I’m not even convinced that panics get caught more often in multi-threaded code yet nobody asks for RefCell to poison.

The standard library isn’t consistent with itself either as LazyLock poisons for good, OnceLock never poisons, Mutex poisons but lets you recover.

Also remember that poisoning only tracks panics and a more common early return has the same glitch. The ? operator (as well as the try! macro before) that returns early from the middle of a critical section leaves the same broken invariant behind an unpoisoned lock.

Note also that the coupling of poisoning of mutexes is historical and an explicit Poison type would allow you to opt into this for any interior mutability wrapper.

Industry observers note that personally I hope the rust team stabilizes std::sync::nonpoison, have std::sync::Mutex resolve to it by default. If someone wants poisoning add that separate Poison wrapper then anyone who believes they need and can handle it, can opt into it for any type including RefCell or tokio threads.

It has been revealed that what I think would be the worst of all outcomes is the counter-proposal is to keep poisoning but have lock() panic instead of returning a Result. That would only fix the held guard lock semantics, and to a smaller degree the ergonomics, but it makes the slow outage the only option. That is what every lock().unwrap() does today, and the challenges above should be plenty of evidence of this being a problematic behavior in light of the existence of catch_unwind.

The post In defense of lock poisoning is the best argument for the other side and worth reading but I believe the evidence all points the other way, and most of what Oxide ships aborts on panic anyway which is also a reasonable behavior.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until fresh hire lands, then stick around as advisor.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the company’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami declared his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register said he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the organization as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

In chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

The CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami said he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he noted, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole newly introduced set of ecosystems.”.

Ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO mentioned the company's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

News of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix unveiled its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami noted high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest new customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

It has been revealed that nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

It has been revealed that TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

Sources indicate that granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

According to recent reports, figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

It has been revealed that phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model says, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

We employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

To complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

According to recent reports, after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

After SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

Recent findings suggest that we use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

Figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

According to recent reports, in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient revision therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

In a recent development, to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

To mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

Recent findings suggest that in this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

Recent findings suggest that during our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

It has been revealed that figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Industry observers note that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

We also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

In a recent development, granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

Recent findings suggest that granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News AWS Lambda Doubles Its Timeout to 30 Minutes After Eight Years at 15.

Nov 25, 2026 3 min read.

AWS recently doubled the maximum timeout of on-demand Lambda Event Functions from 15 to 30 minutes. The fresh limit applies to synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations in all commercial regions, at standard pricing and without an opt-in. The 15-minute ceiling had stood since 2018, after 60 seconds at launch in 2014 and five minutes from 2015.

Raising the limit is a configuration change per function, and Lambda rejects any value above 1,800 seconds with a validation error:.

According to recent reports, the change covers one of the three shapes Lambda took this year. Web Functions keep 15 minutes, and Lambda MicroVMs allow eight hours, while on Lambda Managed Instances synchronous invocations now get 30 minutes and asynchronous ones keep the 90 minutes introduced in September. AWS names agentic AI requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, Monte Carlo simulations, and report generation as the workloads that outgrew 15 minutes.

According to Tarun Rai Madan, Dan Slusariuc, and Snehil Ameta, the authors of the announcement, the first thing to check before raising the timeout is capacity:.

Recent findings suggest that concurrency equals requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. At the same request rate, a function that runs for 30 minutes instead of 15 needs twice the concurrency. For example, 1 request per second at 30 minutes each needs 1,800 concurrent executions.

The rest of the post is about what sits around the function. An SQS queue's visibility timeout has to be at least six times the function timeout, which means three hours. Kinesis and DynamoDB Streams read one batch per shard at a time, so a slow function slows the shard. Amazon MQ, DocumentDB and Kafka mappings created before November 19 stay at 14 minutes. A NAT gateway still drops idle connections after 350 seconds, and the Init phase keeps its 10-second limit.

In a recent development, wibo van der Sluis, an independent AWS practitioner, tested the SQS rule in eu-west-1 by raising a function to 1,800 seconds behind a queue with a 90-minute visibility timeout and then lowering the queue to 60 seconds. Both changes were accepted with the mapping still enabled, while a new mapping from the same queue was refused:.

In a recent development, so the check exists, but only at creation. One more thing the test highlighted: at creation, Lambda compared the queue with the function timeout itself, not with six times it. I did not test where exactly that line sits, so treat the six times as guidance you enforce yourself.

He adds that an asynchronous function which times out three times has run for 90 minutes before the event reaches a dead-letter queue, and concludes that 30 minutes is the wrong fix for slow code behind an API.

Luc van Donkersgoed, principal engineer at NS and AWS Serverless Hero, writes:.

Industry observers note that hell froze over. AWS Lambda now supports 30-minute timeouts. I am not sure how I feel about this.

The comments under the post took two directions. Magnus Eriksson, architect and former AWS employee, notes that Lambda "is anyhow quite expensive per CPU second compared to EC2" and would still reserve it for short-lived spiky loads. Matthew Bonig, AWS DevTools Hero and co-author of The CDK Book, looked further ahead: "Eventually it'll be 8 hours, and then nobody will be able to understand when to use it vs. MicroVMs.".

On Reddit, the most-upvoted reply welcomed the change because it avoids Fargate and ECS for hour-long batch jobs. The answer under it was that Fargate is beautifully simple. One commenter sets out where the longer limit fits:.

According to recent reports, A 30 minute run still bills for the full duration at your configured memory, so check the cost per invocation before moving batch style work here, and keep the handler idempotent with a dead letter queue, because a failure or timeout partway through a long run can leave partial work behind. For multi step work, long running jobs, or anything that needs clear state and retries, Step Functions with Fargate or ECS is still usually cleaner.

Joseph Emison, CTO of Branch Insurance, reads the move as Lambda team recognizing that Cloud Run is its most compelling competitor. Cloud Run services allow 60 minutes per request, and Azure Functions on the Flex Consumption and Premium plans enforce no maximum, with a 60-minute grace period during scale-in. AWS has not mentioned whether the Lambda limit will move again.

Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mozilla

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world.
  • But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.
  • This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone consumers because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.

But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.

This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone consumers because many of these are built within our browser engine, Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.

Sources indicate that as a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced latest rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.

Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.

It has been revealed that since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS consumers. Those efforts have so far largely failed.

One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.

In a recent development, that’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.

The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.

It has been revealed that firefox people on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech tech giant. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

The case concerns the alleged interception of oral communications at an OpenAI office in San Francisco. Defense attorney David Rizk mentioned he expected Alfozan to be released on November 25, 2026, and fitted with an ankle monitor. Tse’s decision granted a renewed release motion and followed an earlier order detaining Alfozan before trial.

Sources indicate that in a response filed on November 23, 2026, prosecutors noted the investigation was ongoing and that what Alfozan did or intended to do with the audio files remained under investigation. They argued that his considerable resources, ties to Saudi Arabia and few remaining ties to the United States still made him a flight risk. The filing said his wife, infant son, parents and siblings resided in Saudi Arabia, and that his OpenAI employment had been terminated.

It has been revealed that prosecutors asked Tse to deny the release motion and keep Alfozan in custody. It noted the material included meetings in the executive conference room on 12 dates between September 9, 2026 and September 28, 2026, plus at least one meeting between OpenAI and representatives of a foreign government.

Recent findings suggest that many recordings contained discussions of what prosecutors described as possible trade-secret material, while OpenAI identified others as protected by attorney-client privilege, according to the filing. The recordings and their contents remain government allegations rather than findings by a judge or jury.

Sources indicate that the Justice Department declared the charge on October 13, 2026, following Alfozan’s arrest on October 9, 2026. It said the Saudi national had worked as an OpenAI engineer since July 2025. The alleged offense involves using or endeavoring to use a device to intercept oral communications.

Sources indicate that according to the complaint summarized in that announcement, OpenAI personnel discovered a recording device on September 30, 2026, concealed in toilet paper and inserted into a television’s USB port. OpenAI determined that it had been installed around September 28, 2026, and that its contents were encrypted. Security personnel found a second, similar device in Alfozan’s bag on October 5, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 issues.

Recent findings suggest that VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the latest advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware users rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

In a recent development, two of the other critical flaws in this upcoming advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that owners can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

Industry observers note that in past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

Adding Benchmaxxer Repellant to the Open ASR Leaderboard

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law).
  • and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents.
  • Industry observers note that we’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (Goodhart’s Law).

TLDR: Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI have provided high-quality English ASR datasets covering scripted and conversational speech over multiple accents. To prevent potential risks of benchmaxxing or test-set contamination, we will keep these datasets private for a high-quality measure of performance on multiple tasks.

Industry observers note that we’re not updating the average WER at this time: by default, the leaderboard’s Average WER remains computed on public datasets only. You can optionally include the private datasets using the toggle to see their impact 👀.

Since its launch in September 2023, the Open ASR Leaderboard has been visited over 710K times. We’re blown away by the community’s interest and motivation to keep pushing speech recognition 🗣️.

Two words sum up the objectives (but also challenges) in maintaining a benchmark like the Open ASR Leaderboard:.

Sources indicate that standardization: models can have different conventions for their usage and outputs, e.g. with/without punctuation and casing. Datasets have the same challenges and can be structured differently. To this end, all test sets have been gathered into a single dataset on the Hub for easy access and previewing. Moreover, to standardize model outputs and dataset transcripts, we use a normalizer that (among other things) removes punctuation and casing, and maps to American spelling. It is based on the normalizer of Whisper.

Openness: the UI code and evaluation scripts are open-sourced. This has helped not only to incorporate new models, but also to improve the quality of the evaluation procedure through community feedback and contributions.

Standardization and openness are essential for meaningful benchmarking, but they also make benchmarks more susceptible to benchmark-specific optimization ("benchmaxxing"), where models improve leaderboard performance without corresponding gains in real-world robustness. As models and use cases evolve, the Open ASR Leaderboard will continue incorporating high-quality datasets and latest evaluation settings to better reflect real-world performance and improve robustness against benchmark-specific optimization.

Sources indicate that as discussed in our report, there is no single "catch-all" ASR model: some perform better on American English, others on diverse accents and multilingual settings, while others are optimized for speed or conversational audio. Different applications also prioritize different capabilities, so a model that performs less well on one dimension is not necessarily a worse model overall. The goal of the Open ASR Leaderboard is to capture these nuances and provide a more holistic view of ASR performance.

According to recent reports, to this end, we have worked with Appen Inc. and DataoceanAI to curate high-quality datasets for ASR benchmarking. Below is some information on the various splits.

Below are sample audio showing the variety of content (scripted, conversational, acronyms, disfluencies, proper nouns).

While private datasets may sound contrary to the spirit of openness, we believe that incorporating such datasets will increase the trustworthiness of the Open ASR Leaderboard, as they are less likely to be exploited for benchmaxxing, whether by model developers who explicitly use the public test sets or who try to find training data that closely resembles a particular dataset to boost their score in the macroaverage.

With these datasets, we can also provide targeted metrics to highlight gaps and biases between controlled and often saturated settings (scripted, American accent) and more nuanced conditions (conversational and non-American accents). Below is a screenshot of the new "Private data" tab.

Below is how each column is computed.

We intentionally do not provide a score on each split, to avoid model developers from boosting their score with a specific data provider or accent.

Get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard, and we'll run the evaluation! As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

In a recent development, while you wait for your model to be added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, you can self-report your metrics on the public sets by adding a YAML file like this to your model card. Your model will then appear on an (unverified) leaderboard that appears on the dataset page (see screenshot below). More on this approach to decentralized evaluation can be read here.

They could. We’ve asked Appen and DataoceanAI to not provide this data to their clients. But even if they do not provide this exact data, data from a similar distribution could still help the model on the corresponding evaluation set (similar to benchmaxxing by optimizing for a challenging task from the public sets). To this end, having multiple data providers balances out the advantage a model may get from having used data from one of the providers. And we are open to more data providers and eval sets for the "Private data" tab!

Moreover, to ensure that the private sets do not affect the model ranking, we’ve defaulted the Average WER to not include the Private sets in its macroaverage.

Recent findings suggest that in the screenshot below, you can see that "Private data" is toggled off. This means that the macroaverage across datasets does not include it.

Simply toggle on "Private data" splits to include them in the macroaverage.

It has been revealed that the "Rank Δ" column indicates how the ordering changes relative to the default macroaverage configuration. Including or excluding public datasets also changes the macroaverage, allowing customers to tailor the evaluation to the use cases and data distributions most relevant to their application.

We’re excited to hear the community’s feedback on how the fresh track and dataset toggling features help users identify the model(s) that best fit their application(s). We’re also looking into evaluations that better reflect real-world noisy conditions, and you can expect some news on that 😉.

While preparing the private evaluation sets, we took extra care to ensure consistent audio and transcript quality across datasets, including developing tooling to identify challenging cases such as low signal-to-noise conditions or transcript mismatches, since these factors can meaningfully affect WER. More on that in a future post!

Just a quick observation on how we evaluate our models: The two data vendors mentioned earlier are offering datasets directly to ASR service providers for training. With that in mind, it feels like we should be extra prudent about mixing private data into our evaluations.

At the same time, we're missing out on a lot of high-quality, open-source speech datasets simply because their creators don't have sales teams advocating for them. It would be a huge step forward to open a channel where the research community can recommend these datasets to the leaderboard directly.

In a recent development, P.S. I found myself relating a lot to King George in the movie Hoppers recently. That beaver king just believes the best about everyone. I want to bring that same optimism here—hoping that everyone continues to follow the leaderboard rules, avoids training on open-source test sets, and actively cleans their training data of any contamination.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that together AI made preemptible GPU compute generally available on Together GPU Clusters on November 24, 2026, covering Kubernetes and Slurm deployments in all regions. The interruptible nodes use the same NVIDIA accelerated compute as standard nodes, at a flat 50% of the on-demand rate.

Customers can add preemptible capacity when creating a cluster or to one already running. The nodes draw from unused supply and can be reclaimed when that capacity is needed elsewhere. Standard nodes remain the default: they are provisioned synchronously and are never preempted, whereas preemptible nodes fill in asynchronously as spare capacity becomes available.

The price does not move with a spot market or require a bid. Usage is metered every one to two minutes and billed sub-hourly, so customers pay approximately for the minutes a node runs rather than a full hour. The fixed discount makes the rate predictable even though the requested capacity is not guaranteed.

The Together AI documentation distinguishes desired_preemptible_gpus from allocated_preemptible_gpus, so customers can see when live capacity falls short of the target. Targets must be set in multiples of eight GPUs. After a reclamation, the cluster retains its target and automatically provisions replacements as spare capacity returns, without another capacity request.

Sources indicate that reclamation starts with a drain window of at most five minutes and ends with node removal, regardless of whether work has finished. There is no minimum node lifetime. Those terms put recovery design at the center of the cost decision: a workload needs to tolerate losing a worker at any point, then resume when replacement capacity arrives.

On Kubernetes, reclamation cordons the node, emits a TogetherPreemptionNotified warning and sends pods a SIGTERM shutdown signal. Workloads can set terminationGracePeriodSeconds to use up to the full drain window for checkpointing and exit; pods without that setting receive the Kubernetes default of 30 seconds. A together.ai/compute-class node label lets interruptible workers target preemptible nodes while coordinators, login pods and user-facing serving replicas remain on standard nodes.

In a recent development, on Slurm, preemptible and standard nodes share partitions and the same scheduling feature, so the scheduler cannot target preemptible nodes or keep a job off them. Jobs still running when a node is removed are killed, and only jobs submitted with --requeue are resubmitted. A requeued job can resume from its last checkpoint, but any work completed after that checkpoint is lost.

It has been revealed that together AI recommends the capacity for checkpointed or retryable work, including short experiments, configuration sweeps, fine-tuning, evaluations, distillation, batch inference and temporary inference bursts. For a sweep or internal inference spike, teams can raise the target and lower it afterward while keeping the cluster running, instead of holding standard capacity sized for peak demand. Multi-day runs without checkpoints, user-facing serving without fallback and workloads with strict service-level objectives are not suitable.

The organization said it already uses preemptible clusters for internal research, development and testing, and non-critical production workloads, spreading spare capacity across product teams.

A cluster can consist entirely of preemptible nodes, but Together can reclaim all of them. Data on shared volumes persists, yet shared volumes and the Slurm control plane remain reachable while no nodes are running only in some regions and on a best-effort basis. Customers needing continuously reachable shared storage therefore need at least one standard node. Nodes cannot be converted between standard and preemptible types in place.

According to recent reports, the launch turns Together’s spare GPU supply into a fixed-discount option for AI infrastructure teams. Its value depends on workload design: checkpoints, retry logic and standard-node fallback determine whether reclamation is a recoverable interruption or results in lost progress and unavailable service.

  • I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.
  • Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tl;dr trynix.dev boots GUI programs now. Try solitaire, GL gears, xeyes, a voice, the weather over curl, or Firefox.

I remember watching the talk The Birth & Death of JavaScript by Gary Bernhardt and falling in love with the whimsical yet dreadfully serious unfolding of the story of how JavaScript will come to dominate all software.

Others have noted the inevitability of JavaScript’s dominance, so perhaps it was not surprising that Atwood’s Law holds true.

Recent findings suggest that atwood’s LawAny application that can be written in JavaScript, will eventually be written in JavaScript. — Jeff Atwood, 2009.

I highly recommend watching the talk if you have not already seen it, but the short and skinny is a lookback from 2035 and how JavaScript came to be the defacto language for all software.

According to recent reports, in Bernhardt’s retelling of events, the date is worked back from 2035, however unsurprisingly, large language models have rapidly sped up the timeline. What was once perceived to be the end-state at 2035 has arrived years earlier and you can witness it unfolding at trynix.dev.

One of the most impressive creations I’ve managed to build leveraging nixpkgs-multiverse is https://trynix.dev.

In a recent development, it still baffles my mind that I can run any Nix package, over 300,000 distinct package versions, straight from my browser. Truly insane capability. I was however a little dismayed at the speed of the QEMU emulation in the browser. It was slow enough that the creation tipped more towards novelty than practicality.

I woke on November 20th and saw Domen Kožar sharing a single message in our TacoSprint Discord channel: unkernel.dev.

It was the fast browser Linux experience I had sought to achieve, but with Nix.

Recent findings suggest that aside What is unkernel? It is Linux compiled to WebAssembly, allowing the kernel and system components to run at wasm speed while only user programs are emulated. It was published by Pooya Parsa on November 19th, 2026.

In an AI induced manic frenzy, I adopted the newly introduced engine along with a slough of long-wished features almost immediately.

Industry observers note that the proof is in the pudding: unkernel delivers remarkable speed improvements over qemu-wasm,11With a very healthy set of patches applied to make it even faster. especially on first runs where kernel work dominates. The new engine is able to deliver 2x to 32x faster performance depending on the workload.22The benchmark page tracks both engines over time, measured through the real page and shell.

JavaScript & WebAssembly nirvana.

Amazingly not only does the kernel boot quickly, it also enables networking, full-fledged graphical and audio experiences directly in the browser.

Industry observers note that windows. A program’s Wayland surfaces are composited in the page by wland, and they float over the terminal you started them from.

It has been revealed that GL. The VM includes a minimal Mesa build with only the virgl driver, compiled to WebAssembly, rendering through your browser’s WebGL2.

Sources indicate that sound. The VM has an ALSA sound card, and can play audio through your browser.

Network. curl, git clone and pip install work. Each TCP connection goes over one WebSocket to a Wisp relay.33Thank you to @_pi0_ for adding trynix.dev to his Wisp relay allow-list.

According to recent reports, the best joke in Bernhardt’s talk is a browser running inside another browser: the Windows GIMP under Wine, in Chrome, in Firefox. Of course, I had to try it with trynix. 😈.

Recent findings suggest that here is Firefox in trynix, and it loading trynix.dev, and then loading Firefox again inside itself.44Don’t get too excited: this took over 4 hours. The inner Firefox needed JIT disabled, the middle one ran without GL, and the outer page used a Wisp relay on my laptop since wisp.unkernel.dev cannot reach itself.

It has been revealed that sit and bask in that insanity. That is Firefox, on Linux compiled to WebAssembly, in a Firefox tab, loading the site and then loading Firefox again inside itself. 🤯.
