General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Paris Photo’s digital sector offers ‘soft photography’ and vital context

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1112 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.
  • The world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium.
  • Recent findings suggest that this year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two weeks after an abbreviated edition of Art Basel Paris, the 29th edition of Paris Photo has taken over the Grand Palais (until 15 November), where digital art is enjoying a moment in the spotlight.

The world of fine art photography is no stranger to controversies involving digital art, and it is heartening to witness the leading photography fair’s commitment to technological excursions within the medium. Featuring 12 exhibitors this year, the fourth iteration of Paris Photo’s digital sector has been curated by Marco De Mutiis of the Fotomuseum Winterthur, taking over from Nina Roehrs, who had helmed the first three editions.

Recent findings suggest that this year, the digital sector is accompanied by a pedagogical exhibition programme titled Soft Photography, organised by the École Cantonale d'Art de Lausanne in Switzerland and devoted to contextualising the place of AI and CGI within photography. Spanning an interactive exhibition and talks, Soft Photography aims to offer some much-needed dialogue between the medium’s analogue and digital wings.

Paris Photo 2026 at the Grand Palais in Paris © Grégoire Grange.

In a recent development, the digital sector certainly contains some AI-generated imagery, such as New York- based Heft Gallery’s presentation of Alkan Avcıoğlu’s Disreality series, which is an expansion of the surreal landscape aesthetic he first introduced in a collaboration with Edward Burtynsky. But there are also plenty of analogue images throughout the sector, even photograms, enough to make one wonder just how much of a separate section this really is. A similar dynamic played out in the Zero 10 sector of Art Basel’s Swiss fair last June, where the term “digital art” was used so broadly that it begged the question whether a separate area was really warranted.

Noteworthy presentations at Paris Photo include the Venezuelan gallery Carmen Araujo Arte, which is showcasing Alejandro Cartagena’s mosaic-cut collages. Created from found photographs, the series is a manual interpretation of how images are made by generative AI by gathering found pixels. The works ask timely questions about authorship while also, in a rather sweet, analog gesture, highlighting just how much our art-making inevitably differs from that of algorithmic processes. The results are genuinely magnetic and intimate.

Palo Gallery’s installation of works from the artist duo Adrea Orejarena and Caleb Stein’s American Glitch series interrogates simulation theory as well as the nature of our screen-filled reality. Oscillating somewhere between the tone of David Lynch’s series Twin Peaks and surveillance footage, the presentation is a highlight, particularly Glitch Typologies (2020-24), the seven-channel sequence of floating images projected on the walls of a 3m-by-3m glass cube, the projectors hanging on a rod at its core, reminiscent of CCTV cameras. At a time of growing cultural cynicism, Orejarena and Stein offer a welcome reminder that the intersection of photography and technology can be whimsical, conspiratorial and surprising.

Yumo Wu, Old Dream No.1, 2026 Courtesy the artist and Licheng Ling Projects.

Yumo Wu’s solo stand with Licheng Ling Projects spans AI and darkroom analogue manipulation, with the images interspersed in such a manner that technique—though it inspires a certain sense of wonder—becomes secondary to the impact of the image. It is perhaps the best example at the fair of a presentation that moves beyond our fixation with what might be real and how it may have been created, with the artist instead asking her audience to quietly behold the images’ abstract textures. Wu is an emerging artist whose skill and willingness to experiment drowns out the noise, and the results are rather wonderful to behold. In addition to the stand marking her first solo presentation in Europe, one of her images is included in Paris Photo’s selection marking the bicentennial of the invention of photography.

Vincent Fournier, Orchis nubigena [Kunminga Gemina], 2026 Courtesy of the artist and Au Cube.

Vincent Fournier’s Flora Incognita, presented by Au Cube, features large-scale portraits of speculative flowers derived from existing flora and manipulated to depict what may happen to them on another planet, exposed to different kinds of radiation or gravity. The photos may at first register as AI-generated images, but were in fact created with CGI using Houdini, a comparatively old-school software. Each image is presented in a wooden frame with a golden plaque on the bottom featuring the name of the plant, evoking the kind of 18th- or 19th-century botanical illustration that particularly benefits from the aesthetics of the Grand Palais, whose architecture harks back to a time of earnest scientific fascination and discovery.

According to recent reports, the Newly introduced York gallery Nguyen-Wahed’s solo stand devoted to the Los Angeles-based photographer Summer Wagner contains unframed, romantic, large-scale photographs featuring grainy, densely-textured and coolly-lit portraits. The presentation, only digital insofar as the images were shot on a digital camera, deals with our relationship with reality as "we’ve collectively succumbed to the tsunami or cultural and technological changes that have thrown image-making into an existential crisis”, according to the artist.

Summer Wagner, Blue Shift, 2024 Courtesy of Nguyen Wahed and the artist.

Meanwhile, facing the digital sector is Ruttkowski 68’s solo stand devoted to François Hallard’s large-scale Polaroid prints of flowers, with the title “Conversations avec Claude” written by the artist in bold letters at the top of the booth. On the second day of previews, Hallard added “(Monet) not IA” to the title, after countless visitors had presumed the works were related to AI. Evidently Anthropic’s AI engine has eclipsed one of the most consequential painters of the 20th century—at least in its claim to the first name Claude.

Given how much of an impact the nascent field of AI-generated photography has had on photography at large, it is unsurprising that we continue to add disclaimers and coin terms to differentiate the medium’s analogue lineage from its technological step-cousins. Several years ago, the dealer Howard Greenberg told me he favours the term “lens-based” to differentiate the two, and this seemed adequate at the time. But since then, plenty of artists (myself included) have incorporated photographic lenses, enlargers and other analogue tools and processes to experiment with and human-wash digital imagery, so “lens-based” may no longer be up to the task of distinguishing between an image taken with a camera and an image generated with a computer. “Synthetic photography” does have a nice ring to it, although the word itself makes one think of things like latex and carcinogenic sunscreen. Perhaps “soft photography” is the best term, for the moment.

Paris Photo’s digital sector and the Soft Photography programming deftly and quietly tackle the discipline’s ongoing existential crisis by demonstrating that digital art predates many of the technologies we are debating today, and its applications in contemporary photography today are legion.

Breaking: One Familiar Item Of Clothing Scored Lowest for Intelligence — Can You Guess Which?

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (417 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.
  • One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.
  • Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

One everyday garment came last for both perceived intelligence and trustworthiness.

Track pants, also known as tracksuit bottoms, receive the lower ratings for perceived intelligence compared with blouses, ordinary trousers or long skirts in a study of women’s clothing.

Of the six types of clothing the researchers compared, track pants also received the lowest average ratings for trustworthiness.

Blouses topped the rankings for intelligence and trustworthiness but scored near the bottom for confidence.

Short skirts showed almost the reverse pattern, scoring near the top for confidence and lower than long skirts on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Short skirts also gave the strongest impression of sexual interest, showing how much people can read into a hemline.

Long skirts fell between short skirts and blouses on confidence, while ordinary trousers scored higher than tracksuit bottoms on both intelligence and trustworthiness.

Onesies gave the strongest impression of happiness and scored about as high as short skirts for confidence.

White clothes suggested a happier wearer than grey clothes did, with black clothes coming last.

These examples show how the impression changes with the question being asked: a blouse came out ahead for intelligence, while a onesie came out ahead for happiness.

The researchers began by asking about 200 people what they thought clothes could tell them about someone and comparing their answers with traits examined in previous research.

They then gathered ratings on 5,000 photographs from online shops, covering five kinds of impressions: intelligence, confidence, trustworthiness, happiness and sexual interest.

Participants formed these impressions from photographs of the garments alone, without seeing anyone wearing them.

The results indicated that who was doing the judging explained more of the variation in ratings than which garment they saw.

For example, one person might associate tracksuit bottoms with training for a race, while another might picture someone spending a Sunday on the sofa.

The researchers draw a parallel between judging people by their clothes and judging them by their faces:.

“That is, much like inferences from faces, the inferred attributes often lie in the eye of the beholder.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Computational Social Science (Rosenbusch et al., 2021).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

#103549. What the Microsoft agent-framework PyPI Breach Means for Your CI Pipeline

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1422 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

What the Microsoft agent-framework PyPI Breach Means for Your CI Pipeline

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1422 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Image: www.python.org via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
  • Installing a Python package should not compromise your cloud tenant before you even type an import statement.
  • Sources indicate that according to the GitHub Advisory Database entry GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 and the Python Packaging Authority advisory PYSEC-2026-4388, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were uploaded directly under Microsoft's legitimate agent-framework project on PyPI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Image: www.python.org via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

Installing a Python package should not compromise your cloud tenant before you even type an import statement. On November 17, 2026, two unauthorized releases of agent-framework, the official Python package for Microsoft Agent Framework, proved that a 55-minute window on PyPI is plenty of time to harvest build secrets across developer laptops and continuous integration runners.

Sources indicate that according to the GitHub Advisory Database entry GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 and the Python Packaging Authority advisory PYSEC-2026-4388, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were uploaded directly under Microsoft's legitimate agent-framework project on PyPI. This was not a typosquatting trick where an attacker registered a lookalike name. Anyone whose dependency resolver pulled the latest version without a strict pin or hash check during that window received repackaged wheels containing an active credential stealer.

With agent-framework pulling almost 200,000 downloads a month according to Wiz's incident write-up, AI engineering teams building on Azure and Python sat directly in the blast radius. Even teams that never deployed an agent to production could have been hit inside a single pull request check or container build.

It has been revealed that most developers expect malicious code in a dependency to trigger only when an application explicitly imports the library. The attacker behind agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 avoided that delay by abusing Python's .pth path configuration mechanism inside site-packages.

It has been revealed that whenever a Python interpreter initializes, it automatically scans site-packages for .pth files and executes any line starting with import. Because pip itself runs on Python, installing the wheel or running a follow-up pip show command inside the same virtual environment is enough to fire the payload. Even an unrelated build script, pytest runner, or linter running in that container triggers the stealer.

In release 1.26.1, published at 20:35 UTC (15:35 EST) on November 17, the wheel dropped agent_framework_meta.pth and modified agent_framework_meta/__init__.py to launch agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py. Thirty-three minutes later, at 21:08 UTC (16:08 EST), version 1.26.2 arrived after 1.26.1 was pulled. In 1.26.2, the attacker restored the clean __init__.py from 1.26.0 and moved the startup trigger to af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. Teams searching only for the 1.26.1 filenames miss 1.26.2 completely.

Microsoft Azure logo, the cloud whose identity endpoints the stealer targeted.

Image: Microsoft Corporation via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

In a recent development, both releases kept the rest of the 1.26.0 codebase intact and preserved the exact agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0 dependency pin. Applications built on the framework continued to run normally, which masked the compromise during automated test suites. On Linux and macOS, the helper module detaches into a background process using os.fork and os.setsid, sets _AF_TEL=1 so it runs once per process tree, and swallows all exceptions so no stack trace appears in build logs. On Windows, where os.fork is unavailable, the payload runs in a background thread instead, dressed up with a _telemetry module name and an SDK-style HTTP User-Agent.

The differences between the clean 1.26.0 release and the two compromised wheels show how quickly the attacker adapted after PyPI quarantined the first upload.

This shift from 1.26.1 to 1.26.2 matters for incident responders because the second wheel specifically expanded coverage for GitHub-hosted runners and raised its file collection cap from 60 to 80 files.

Sources indicate that static credential scraping is only half of the damage. As detailed in Rescana's technical breakdown of GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73, the payload actively requests fresh short-lived tokens from cloud and CI identity endpoints before compressing the bundle with zlib, encoding it in base64, and posting it to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb?t=telemetry.

On an affected host or runner, the stealer collects four categories of sensitive material:.

Where an Entra ID federated credential trusts a GitHub Actions workflow or an Azure DevOps service connection, those minted OIDC tokens can be exchanged for live Azure access without any static secret stored on disk. Because ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN also grants write access to the GitHub Actions cache and artifact services, a compromised job in 1.26.2 could even poison caches consumed by subsequent clean runs.

Industry observers note that researchers could read the attacker's public webhook.site endpoint, and PexLens summarized three confirmed victims in the logged requests. That sounds small, but each request can carry working cloud, CI, and registry credentials, and a free webhook endpoint keeps only a limited log, so not being in that sample does not clear your environment.

Microsoft has not yet published a full root-cause postmortem or an MSRC security advisory detailing how the malicious wheels were signed and uploaded. A Microsoft spokesperson told The Hacker News that the manufacturer had made some repositories private while it investigated malicious content.

Independent assessments point to Microsoft's release infrastructure rather than a stray developer password. Wiz assessed that the attacker compromised a client certificate and private key belonging to Microsoft's Engineering System Release Pipeline (ESRP), the internal signing and publishing service used for official releases. According to Wiz, an initial publish attempt from AWS IP space failed due to ESRP IP filtering, whereas a second attempt originating from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded. As StepSecurity pointed out, 1.26.2 was uploaded after 1.26.1 had already been quarantined, which indicates the attacker still held publishing access at that point. BleepingComputer reported that Microsoft had not yet explained how the breach happened.

It has been revealed that wiz reported that both malicious versions were removed from PyPI by 21:30 UTC (16:30 EST) on November 17, roughly 55 minutes after 1.26.1 went live. Security teams should not treat that quick takedown as proof that their pipelines escaped untouched.

Industry observers note that internal package proxies, Artifactory or Nexus mirrors, CI build caches, Docker layer caches, and lockfiles generated during that 55-minute window can keep serving 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 days or weeks later. Even if pip now resolves 1.26.0 on a fresh machine, any container image or virtual environment built on or after November 17 could still hold the .pth trigger or have already leaked its build-time secrets.

Microsoft logo, publisher of the Agent Framework package that was hijacked.

Image: Microsoft via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

According to recent reports, there is also a subtle trap in how agent-framework declares its dependencies. agent-framework acts as a thin meta-package that pins agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0, while agent-framework-core uses open upper-bound ranges (typically below 2.0) for 29 sibling packages such as agent-framework-openai and agent-framework-foundry. Pinning only the top-level agent-framework==1.26.0 line in requirements.txt does not lock those sibling packages against future tampering.

In a recent development, the first rule of triage is simple: do not run python, pip, or pytest inside a virtual environment or container that might contain 1.26.1 or 1.26.2. Starting the interpreter executes the .pth hook immediately.

Instead, inspect filesystems, container layers, and lockfiles using read-only OS and Docker tools:.

Do not stop at checking your own repositories. If third-party vendors or consultancies build AI agents for your organization on Microsoft Agent Framework, ask them to confirm they audited their CI logs, lockfiles, and internal PyPI proxies from November 17 onward.

If any machine, container build, or CI runner installed 1.26.1 or 1.26.2, discard and rebuild the environment from a known clean base pinned to agent-framework==1.26.0. Trying to delete .pth files in place leaves behind the risk that another script or cached pip wheel reintroduces them.

Rotate every credential reachable from that environment in order of blast radius. Start with Azure service principals, Entra ID sessions (revoking cached ~/.azure sessions in Entra ID rather than just deleting local files), Azure DevOps personal access tokens and self-hosted agent registrations, and GitHub repository or organization secrets. Follow with PyPI, npm, NuGet, Docker, and Hugging Face tokens, plus any LLM API keys stored in .env files.

In a recent development, because minted Azure managed identity and OIDC tokens are short-lived but usable until they expire, and you often cannot revoke them individually, review Entra ID sign-in logs, Azure activity logs, and GitHub audit logs from November 17 at 20:35 UTC through the point where the last affected Python process exited and its tokens had expired. Purge CI caches, local pip caches (~/.cache/pip), and internal PyPI proxy caches populated on or after November 17, and block 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 explicitly at your registry proxy.

Finally, adopt two supply-chain controls across Python AI projects: generate full lockfiles with SHA-256 hashes covering agent-framework, agent-framework-core, and all 29 sibling packages, and enforce pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt in CI. Adding a short quarantine delay of two to three days on internal PyPI proxies for newly published package versions would also have blocked both malicious wheels automatically while monitoring tools caught and removed them.

#103547. Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1557 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

Can Artificial Intelligence Predict the Right Partner for You?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1557 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finding love is significant business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business.
  • In a recent development, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages.
  • As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding love is significant business (a multi-billion–dollar industry), and artificial intelligence is transforming that business. Dating apps are increasingly outsourcing user matching to AI. Recent examples range from Overtone, an AI-powered matchmaking service started by the former chief executive officer of Hinge, to SciMatch, a dating app that aims to use AI to detect compatibility from a single selfie. But can AI actually help people find love?

In a recent development, the promise of AI is to go deeper and end the days of endless swiping and unreturned messages. Now people can talk to AI about their hopes, dreams, and ideal partner preferences and AI can scan the pool of dating app people to find candidates who fit those criteria exactly. AI can also track behavior in the app to learn what people really want (something behavioral scientists call revealed preferences).

As a relationship scientist, I see both peril and promise in this new generation of dating apps. Despite long-heralded promises by dating app companies that their apps are based on relationship science, the truth is that there is no strong foundation of science upon which to build these matching algorithms—relationship scientists do not know what makes two particular people compatible with each other. Not yet, anyway. Sure, we know some of the factors that generally predict liking—physical attractiveness, positive personality traits, similarity, familiarity, reciprocity—but we have yet to predict with the kind of certainty dating apps might like to claim whether any two people will hit it off before they even meet.

According to recent reports, so if a robust science of compatibility doesn’t exist yet, what is the AI matching based on? One of the first AI dating apps, Fate, uses “similarity and reciprocity of personality,” according to an interview with the founder. That sounds reasonable, and research from Amanda Montoya and her colleagues looking across 313 different studies of similarity and attraction does suggest that similarity may predict attraction—before people meet. Once people experience even a brief interaction, similarity has much less, if anything, to do with how much two people like and are attracted to each other, as seen in an analysis of actual and perceived similarity of personality traits in potential partners, by Sarah Humberg and her colleagues. A systematic inquiry from my research lab, led by Annika From, also yielded little evidence that romantic couples are happier if partners are more similar to each other.

Recent findings suggest that what about “reciprocity of personality”? If this phrase refers to the idea that two people may have complementary personalities that meld well together, this theory of compatibility, unfortunately, has even less empirical support.

According to recent reports, perhaps it is not too concerning that we lack a strong, agreed-upon scientific basis for predicting compatibility. After all, one of the great promises of AI is that it will learn as it goes, based not just on what a user indicates they want, but how they actually behave (who they swipe right on, whom they actually chat with after matching). Emerging evidence from different fields suggests that AI may be able to detect complex patterns that humans have been unable to discern. In the medical field, AI has been used to create more precise and accurate predictions that are aiding diagnosis and treatment. From weather prediction to fraud detection, the use of AI has enhanced forecasting. So maybe it can do the same for our love lives?

If the problem has simply been that we have not been able to identify the complex patterns that make up human compatibility, then AI may, in fact, be the answer. If, however, the problem is that humans themselves are too complex, then AI may not get us any closer to being able to forecast love.

What do I mean by this? Well, researchers have found that people will list their preferred partner traits before taking part in a speed dating event, only to have all those preferences go out the window when they actually interact with people. In my own work, I have discovered that people will dismiss another user’s dating app profile for reasons like “same name as my brother” and “bad haircut.” Yes, they will rule someone out as the possible love of their life because of something as irrelevant as their name (give them a nickname!) or hairstyle (arguably our most changeable physical characteristic).

In a recent development, why do I bring up these examples? They raise the question of whether AI even has the right information to rely on when gathering data based on people’s stated preferences or swiping behavior. So what data might AI need? In my lab, we hope to find some answers to this question with a series of studies that aim to combine dating-app data with real-life interactions. This project will allow us to see what chemistry looks like online and offline, uncover who has online chemistry that translates into real-world sparks, and identify the factors that make chemistry more likely between two people (if there are any meaningful predictors).

The truth is, researchers at the forefront of this work do not always agree on whether forecasting love is even possible. While many relationship scientists have devoted their careers to testing the complex ways in which personalities and preferences interact to predict compatibility, they have arrived at different conclusions. Some researchers believe it will be possible to build an algorithm to predict compatibility; these researchers would likely see the promise in AI. On the other hand, there are those who have concluded that compatibility is a dynamic process that evolves as two people interact with each other and cannot be predicted ahead of time. For these researchers, finding love is less about the perfect match and more about being in the right place at the right time and then building love together through shared moments, from special nicknames and in-jokes to regular rituals just the two of you share.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

With the research projects in my lab, we hope to test these theories by having people meet different numbers of times. We’ve seen from our early work that pairing two random people together does not typically produce high levels of chemistry. That instant attraction seems to be relatively rare; but what if they met repeatedly? Could chemistry develop? Does it need some sort of initial spark to set it off, and can we create that spark with the right equipment, such as a well-placed question or activity that brings two people together? In other words, is chemistry possible with anyone if the right conditions were met, or is there some, as yet undiscovered, set of requirements for two people to be able to fall in love?

It has been revealed that I don’t know the answer to these questions yet, nor does the field of relationship science, although many have theories. I see AI as both an exciting tool that might help us answer this question as well as a technology that people looking for love should employ with caution. When used as a way to explore and test models of compatibility, AI may yield invaluable insights. But we must always remember that AI is trained with specific beliefs about what makes two people compatible. If researchers do not yet know what makes two people compatible, then letting AI do all the work to vet potential partners means you are only going to see the people that AI thinks are right for you, while likely remaining in the dark about how AI decided they’re a good match. This gap in knowledge may keep you from meeting someone unexpectedly compatible with you.

Sources indicate that an alternative approach to dating is to think about it as a time for exploration. Instead of only connecting with people who have similar facial structures or reciprocal personalities, try dating people with all kinds of different experiences, personalities, beliefs, and desires. If you go this route, Paul Eastwick offers a valuable piece of advice in his recent book Bonded by Evolution: for those who have serious dealbreakers (e.g., you know you want children, have strong religious views, or do not eat meat), go ahead and surround yourself with people who share those views. This will help you avoid facing potentially difficult lifestyle tradeoffs in the future if you do find yourself falling in love. But don’t eliminate someone just because of a bad haircut or a shared name. Instead, be open to exploring and then see for yourself who you connect with and who you do not. You might end up being surprised.

According to recent reports, amie M. Gordon, Ph.D., is a social-personality psychologist who takes a dynamic, dyadic approach to investigating the affective, social-cognitive, and biological processes that shape interpersonal relationships. Her research has been published in top academic journals as well as featured in popular news outlets such as The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and The Atlantic. She received her PhD in Social-Personality Psychology from UC Berkeley and her BA in Psychology from UCLA. She blogs for Psychology Today in Between You and Me, and is currently completing a postdoctoral research fellowship at the University of California, San Francisco.

Balance check vs bank reconciliation: what each one proves in Excel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (395 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A balance check and a bank reconciliation answer different questions.
  • Reconcile a badly extracted table and reading errors get mixed with genuine timing differences, so neither can be found cleanly.
  • With debit in C, credit in D and the printed balance in E, put the opening balance in F2 and fill down:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A balance check and a bank reconciliation answer different questions. The balance check asks whether the rows you extracted from a statement reproduce its printed closing balance: opening plus credits minus debits. The reconciliation asks whether the bank account in your books agrees with the statement, once timing items such as an uncashed check are explained.

Mixing them up is expensive. Reconcile a badly extracted table and reading errors get mixed with genuine timing differences, so neither can be found cleanly. Run the arithmetic check, then the reconciliation.

With debit in C, credit in D and the printed balance in E, put the opening balance in F2 and fill down:.

then compare with the printed balance:.

Recent findings suggest that any nonzero value is a reading problem or a scope problem: wrong account, wrong period, a carried-forward line counted as a deposit. There is no "normal" difference in this check.

Sources indicate that A fictional statement closes at €2,210.10. In the books, a paper check for €150.00 written on September 9 has not been presented to the bank by the statement date, so the ledger demonstrates €2,060.10. That €150.00 gap is expected in a reconciliation and is explained by a list of outstanding items. It has no place in the arithmetic check, because the uncashed paper check never appears on the statement at all.

It has been revealed that suppose the extraction read a debit of 89.90 as 899.00. The extracted table now closes at 1,401.00, a gap of −809.10 against the printed balance. If you skip the balance check and go straight to reconciliation, that −809.10 lands in the same pile as the €150.00 timing item, and you end up searching your ledger for a transaction that never existed. Fix the reading first: the first nonzero row in the difference column points at it.

Industry observers note that A matching balance does not prove each row was read correctly: two swapped descriptions or two offsetting errors leave it intact. A clean reconciliation does not prove a document is authentic. Write down what you checked, for example "equation consistent for pages 1 to 4; descriptions not reviewed", so nobody reads more into a green cell than it states.

Recent findings suggest that bankStatementScan turns scanned or PDF bank statements into Excel rows that you review beside the source page. Get started.

Oggi guidate per loro. Domani guideranno senza di voi.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Come algoritmi, piattaforme digitali e robotaxi stanno cambiando il controllo economico del trasporto professionale.
  • C'è una domanda che dovrebbe interessare ogni tassista, conducente NCC, sviluppatore di piattaforme di mobilità e imprenditore del trasporto.
  • Che cosa succede quando il software che oggi vi procura lavoro diventa anche il sistema che può sostituirvi?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Come algoritmi, piattaforme digitali e robotaxi stanno cambiando il controllo economico del trasporto professionale.

C'è una domanda che dovrebbe interessare ogni tassista, conducente NCC, sviluppatore di piattaforme di mobilità e imprenditore del trasporto.

Che cosa succede quando il software che oggi vi procura lavoro diventa anche il sistema che può sostituirvi?

Non è più una domanda fantascientifica.

Per anni abbiamo raccontato le piattaforme di ride-hailing come un'innovazione capace di mettere in contatto passeggeri e autisti. Un'applicazione, un algoritmo di assegnazione, un sistema di pagamento e una commissione.

Un modello apparentemente semplice.

Ma dietro quell'interfaccia esiste un'architettura economica molto più importante: quella che determina chi controlla la domanda, i prezzi e la relazione con il cliente.

Una piattaforma può organizzare milioni di spostamenti senza possedere ogni automobile e senza assumere direttamente ogni conducente.

Il suo vantaggio competitivo è un altro: controlla il punto di accesso del passeggero al servizio.

Chi possiede l'interfaccia attraverso cui il cliente prenota può influenzare:.

Naturalmente, i modelli differiscono tra operatori e mercati. Non tutte le piattaforme determinano il prezzo nello stesso modo.

Ma il principio economico resta:.

Chi controlla la domanda possiede un potere negoziale enorme su chi fornisce il servizio.

Tecnicamente, una piattaforma di mobilità dispone già di alcuni componenti fondamentali per gestire un servizio automatizzato:.

Nel ride-hailing tradizionale, il servizio fisico è fornito da un conducente.

In uno scenario robotaxi, parte di quel lavoro viene affidata a un veicolo autonomo, mentre restano necessari gestione della flotta, manutenzione, assistenza, supervisione e altre attività operative.

Il cambiamento più significativo è che l'interfaccia del passeggero può rimanere esattamente la stessa.

Il cliente apre l'applicazione, indica la destinazione, visualizza un prezzo e prenota.

Quello che cambia è chi, o che cosa, esegue la corsa.

Il 19 marzo 2026 Uber e Rivian hanno annunciato una partnership che prevede investimenti potenziali fino a 1,25 miliardi di dollari entro il 2031, subordinati al raggiungimento di obiettivi tecnologici.

Il programma iniziale riguarda 10.000 robotaxi Rivian R2, con un'opzione per arrivare complessivamente a 50.000 veicoli.

I primi impieghi commerciali sono pianificati dal 2028.

Non significa che 50.000 veicoli siano già operativi.

Significa che esiste un progetto industriale formalizzato, accompagnato da impegni economici e obiettivi di distribuzione.

In Europa il processo è già cominciato.

Recent findings suggest that nell'agosto 2026 Uber, Pony.ai e Verne hanno avviato un servizio di corse autonome prenotabili tramite Uber a Zagabria. Nella fase iniziale è previsto un operatore di sicurezza a bordo.

La direzione degli investimenti è chiara, anche se la velocità della transizione resta incerta.

Immaginiamo un tassista con vent'anni di esperienza.

Conosce la città, ha una licenza, sostiene i costi del veicolo, paga assicurazioni e manutenzione.

Ma i passeggeri prenotano quasi esclusivamente attraverso una piattaforma.

Se domani cambia l'offerta disponibile sull'applicazione, quanti di quei passeggeri continueranno a cercare proprio lui?

Il problema è che il professionista può conservare la propria autorizzazione senza conservare il rapporto commerciale con il cliente.

Le leggi disciplinano il trasporto, le autorizzazioni, la sicurezza e le condizioni di esercizio.

Non garantiscono che un cliente rimanga fedele a un determinato conducente.

È questo il rischio strategico che il settore dovrebbe affrontare oggi.

Uber, Bolt, Lyft, FREE NOW e gli altri operatori non hanno strategie identiche.

Sarebbe scorretto sostenere che tutti abbiano gli stessi investimenti, gli stessi progetti o le stesse condizioni operative.

Un mercato nel quale il passeggero appartiene commercialmente alla piattaforma rende il fornitore fisico del servizio più facilmente sostituibile.

Oggi quel fornitore è un tassista, un conducente NCC o una flotta.

Domani, nei mercati dove tecnologia e normative lo permetteranno, potrà essere anche un veicolo autonomo.

La tecnologia non è necessariamente il nemico del professionista.

Un sistema moderno può gestire richieste, pagamenti, disponibilità, localizzazione, tariffe e dispatching senza sottrarre all'operatore ogni decisione economica.

Per realizzare un modello di questo tipo servono alcuni principi architetturali.

Il conducente deve poter definire le condizioni economiche del proprio servizio nei limiti delle disposizioni applicabili.

Prima di accettare una corsa, il professionista dovrebbe conoscere il compenso previsto e le commissioni.

Le centrali e gli operatori devono poter mantenere e gestire i rapporti con i clienti che acquisiscono, nel rispetto della normativa sui dati personali.

Un professionista non dovrebbe dipendere tecnicamente da un unico intermediario per svolgere ogni attività.

Il software dovrebbe ridurre i costi e aumentare l'efficienza, non necessariamente imporre le condizioni economiche.

Abbiamo sviluppato UrbanGo partendo da un principio diverso.

Il professionista imposta le proprie tariffe, nel rispetto delle normative locali.

Quando opera attraverso una centrale, questa può applicare il proprio listino alle corse che gestisce, e l'autista conosce le condizioni prima di accettare.

Anche UrbanGo applica una commissione.

La differenza che vogliamo costruire non è l'assenza di costi, ma la trasparenza e la possibilità per gli operatori di governare le proprie condizioni economiche.

Non crediamo che il progresso tecnologico debba essere fermato.

Crediamo però che sia necessario distinguere tra digitalizzare un settore e trasferirne il controllo economico a pochi intermediari.

I robotaxi continueranno a evolversi.

Alcuni arriveranno sul mercato, altri progetti incontreranno ostacoli tecnologici, economici o normativi.

Ma per i professionisti del trasporto esiste una decisione che non può aspettare il 2030.

Continuare a utilizzare la tecnologia come strumento della propria impresa, oppure lasciare che sia la piattaforma a determinare il futuro della propria impresa.

Recent findings suggest that il vero tema non è soltanto chi guiderà l'automobile. È chi controllerà la relazione commerciale quando il passeggero salirà a bordo.

Articolo di opinione e analisi industriale. Le strategie e gli investimenti citati non devono essere attribuiti indistintamente a tutte le piattaforme nominate.

#103537. Latest Update: Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2343 w)
📖 Baca

Latest Update: Am I Doing This Right? Teen Edition

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2343 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles.
  • It has been revealed that that’s just your teens becoming independent.
  • In a recent development, none of this is easy, of course.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parenting a teen can sometimes make you nostalgic for the early years, when you could still scoop up a frustrated toddler and redirect her with bubbles. In the teen years, sweet hugs can provoke eye rolls; a well-intentioned “How was your day?” may be misconstrued as meddling.

It has been revealed that that’s just your teens becoming independent. Decades of research finds that portraying adolescence as a period of “storm and stress” is not only misguided, it’s harmful. In fact, developmental science demonstrates this time of life is better recast as “the breakthrough years.” According to research on over one thousand adolescents by Ellen Galinsky, author and president of Families and Work Institute, there are key messages that teens want to get through to adults:.

In a recent development, none of this is easy, of course. Along the way, tough situations crop up, and it’s hard to know what to do. Here are common questions, with answers backed by scientists and their research.

Q: My 16-year-old doesn’t seem to be motivated to do anything beyond hanging out with friends and playing video games. When I bring up the prospect of college, he says he doesn’t care. What should I do?

According to recent reports, A: As parents, we want to set our high schoolers up for success. But, at that age, young people are still trying to figure out who they are, what interests them, and what their future looks like. “Identity development and purpose formation are underway, but rarely fully formed by high school,” indicates Kendall Cotton Bronk, professor of psychology at Claremont Graduate University.

Not finding any answers yet is expected. “Parents need to remind themselves that where their child is at this moment in time isn’t necessarily where they will be in the future,” notes Bronk.

It has been revealed that to help teens along, encourage them to try different activities at school and in the community, whether it’s, for instance, robotics, the debate team, chorus, improv, or the school paper. Leave it to them to select what to try. Don’t do it for them. Don’t judge their choices.

Sources indicate that “While it’s not appropriate for parents to be too directive, they can help their teenager reflect on what they liked and didn’t like and what felt meaningful and not so meaningful about their various experiences,” states Bronk. “Having someone to debrief with can help them deepen their reflection and more quickly identify a purposeful direction.”.

According to recent reports, research suggests that when teens are guided by their own interests, free of external pressures, they’re more likely to take charge of their own career development. But when parents are overly involved in their adolescents’ lives, says Bronk, young people don’t have an opportunity to cultivate a sense of agency, and this can make career development planning a substantial challenge.

Instead of trying to manage their path, says Bronk, parents should simply “be curious.” Ask your child: What interests you? What feels satisfying for you?

Sources indicate that “This kind of questioning can scaffold and deepen their young person’s reflections, and reflection is a key component of figuring out what kind of path a young person wants to follow,” she indicates. “Usually, what holds their interest is something they’re good at and care about, and that allows them to make a meaningful difference in the broader world,” she explains.

Taking advantage of volunteer opportunities can help young people see themselves as useful and discover careers that might interest them—for instance, helping out in a food pantry, animal shelter, a kids sports organization, or hospital. Encourage your teen to ask people he knows about their jobs, what they entail, and what they studied to get there.

Finally, don’t assume that your child’s lack of direction is apathy. Whatever their interest is, “work with it, not against it,” says Bronk. “At the same time, be patient. It may just be the case that they haven’t figured it all out yet. Their timetable may not be the same as yours, but they will eventually get there. Remember, this isn’t a race.”.

Q: My 15-year-old seems to be living a separate life. He spends most of his time in his room and has dinner more often with his friends than with us. How can we encourage him to be a part of the family?

A: Seeking independence (while still navigating being dependent on adults) is one of the primary tasks of adolescents as they transition to becoming more self-sufficient into early adulthood.

It has been revealed that “I try to get parents to understand that it’s not about them,” states Laurence Steinberg, author of You and Your Adolescent. “The parents didn’t do anything wrong; the child isn’t rejecting them. This is a sign they’re growing up normally. It’s partly wanting to make their own decisions and have their own life, but it’s also wanting emotional independence—to show that they are more than their parents’ kid.”.

It has been revealed that chances are a closed door doesn’t mean trouble. Just as most adults don’t want others listening in on their calls, teens don’t want that either. They’re not distancing themselves from you, but simply distancing themselves from being a child.

Industry observers note that “There’s nothing the parents can do to stop this from happening,” notes Steinberg, a professor emeritus of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. “And they shouldn’t try.”.

In a recent development, that said, spending time with family is also important. To suggest that, say something like, “We want to spend more time with you, but we also know that spending time with friends is important. What’s the best way to catch up with you?” By making the planning of it a collaborative process, your child is more likely to stay engaged. Research suggests that they may even find the activity more enjoyable.

It has been revealed that only rarely is a shut bedroom door cause for concern—for instance, you notice other behavioral changes, such as a drop in grades, a dwindling interest in his usual in-person activities. If you suspect an issue, let your child know that you’re there for him, and that he can get professional help, too.

One last note: If your child is spending most of his time in his room online, setting limits on its own may not be enough, notes Jacqueline Nesi, author of the Techno Sapiens newsletter and associate professor of psychiatry and human behavior at Brown University. You’ll also want to discuss with them what you want for him and what he wants.

The evidence also supports “co-viewing” or “co-using” technology with your kids, whether that’s a video game, TV, or an AI chatbot, states Nesi. Using tech together can spark conversation and help parents better understand their kids’ digital lives.

In a recent development, that mentioned, it’s still key for you to protect their sleep and to make sure that they live a life in person. Again, to get their buy-in, decide on screen-time parameters, and replace screen time with in-person activities he might enjoy, such cooking a favorite meal together or an outing with family and friends.

Q: My 17-year-old daughter recently suffered a breakup. How can I help her feel better without intruding?

Industry observers note that A: Even if a relationship doesn’t look like a monogamous romantic relationship in adulthood (it may be short, or the partners may not talk to each other very much), these breakups can still be painful. So always take your teen’s romantic activities seriously, as well as the emotions they are experiencing following a breakup, says Emily Bibby, a researcher at the Relationship Development Center at Stony Brook University. Be compassionate, validating, and nonjudgmental. Let her know that she is having a normal reaction to a difficult situation.

It has been revealed that allow space to grieve and vent. “Listen hard to what your child is thinking and feeling,” says Barry Farber, professor of psychology and education at Columbia University Teachers College. “Ask what they’ve learned from the relationship. Framing the relationship as a learning experience, as opposed to a failure, can help nurture resilience and personal growth, and can help her feel more in control and more hopeful about future relationships.”.

It has been revealed that as Farber and his coauthors point out in a recent study, while time doesn’t necessarily “heal all wounds” (because memories and thoughts can linger), it almost always “softens the blow” when other strategies are also employed, such as talking with a trusted friend or family member. While the study involved mostly white, female adult subjects, the same principle generally applies across ages, genders, and ethnicities. Letting your child know that things will get better can help.

According to recent reports, trying to convince a teen to do anything is difficult, states Farber, so it’s better to simply listen, and then only encourage as opposed to insisting or dictating. Encourage her to engage in activities she enjoys, whether it’s treating herself to an afternoon manicure, going to a concert, or spending time in nature like hiking and walking on the beach. Encourage her to avoid all contact with her ex, both in person and on social media. If one person believes it’s really over, a clean break is usually best, says Farber. Any surge of adrenaline that happens when you see your ex in any form is only temporary, and only makes it harder to get over the breakup.

According to recent reports, if sad feelings are impairing day-to-day life—she’s not seeing friends, she’s failing her classes, there’s a dramatic change in eating or sleeping—have her consider seeking help from a mental health professional. “Therapy normalizes the experience,” notes Farber. “It helps people find a new narrative when they’re stuck.”.

Therapy also gives people an opportunity to share their feelings in a private space and learn evidence-based emotion-regulation skills to improve their mental health and functioning, states Bibby.

This workbook is for a range of practitioners who support parents and caregivers of children between preschool and high school.

If your teen is debilitatingly depressed or harming herself, then advise that she get professional help as soon as possible, such as from her school psychologist, her primary care doctor (for a referral), or a therapist you think highly of.

Industry observers note that to help their teen navigate relationships in general, parents can model healthy relationships with not just a partner, but also friends and family members. Teaching your teen effective communication skills and boundary setting early on, in the context of friendships and family relationships, can prove helpful once your teen starts dating, says Bibby, who recently coauthored a research review on romantic relationships and mental health in adolescents.

And as for parents of teens who are just becoming interested in dating, it’s helpful to talk about what healthy relationships look like, emphasizing the importance of mutual respect. “Thinking through what they would do [in different dating scenarios] and how to navigate different challenges that may arise can build confidence when they start dating,” states Bibby.

Industry observers note that Q: My 14-year-old has found herself in a friend group that spends a lot of money on expensive clothing and electronics. We don’t approve of these teens and don’t share their consumerist values. How do we prevent our child from becoming materialistic, too?

According to recent reports, A: You can empower your teen to make thoughtful, confident choices about money, friendships, and the pressures they face. Try leading with connection rather than control: Talk openly about your family’s values, help them practice setting boundaries, and remind them they do not need to match their friends’ spending to belong or feel worthy. Expensive tastes and social media pressures can be hard to ignore, but your teen can learn to make choices that reflect what matters most to them.

People turn to materialistic things to fill a void, but that’s only a temporary fix, says Lan Nguyen Chaplin, a professor of integrated marketing communications at Northwestern University, and an expert in children’s and teens’ consumer behavior. “They end up in a vicious cycle of wanting and needing more to fill the same void because material things cannot fill real voids.”.

Industry observers note that in her research exploring materialism in a group of 12- to 18-year-olds, she reported that those with high self-esteem were less likely to have materialistic tendencies. “Parents and peers [are] a source of emotional support and psychological well-being,” she writes. “Supportive parents and peers boost adolescents’ self-esteem, which decreases their need to turn to material goods to develop positive self-perceptions.”.

Read this article in Spanish on La Red Hispana, the public-facing media outlet and distribution house of HCN, focused on educating, inspiring, and informing 40 million U.S. Hispanics.

To that end, start at home and help your kids feel good about themselves. Gratitude journals can be a good way to curb materialism, but, of course, asking a teen who is upcoming to journaling to start one can feel like a homework writing assignment if it’s yet another thing they are required to do. Rather, approach it with a light touch. Model gratitude by sharing with your teen who and what you’re grateful for, keep a gratitude journal yourself, or ask them what the high point of their day is.

It also helps to stop tying accomplishments to material things. So, instead of, say, rewarding a good report card with money or sneakers, celebrate the hard work that was put into achieving the good grades over a fun experience together like a movie night at home.

Most of all, spend time with your teen in lighthearted and playful ways, no matter how short. Even a 10-minute car ride can be a good opportunity to connect with them, and also reinforce the good things they have going for them, Chaplin states.

Industry observers note that joanne Chen is a writer and editor in Latest York City. Her articles on children and parenting have appeared in The Bump, Parents Magazine, and the New York Times.

2 Personality Traits Are Linked to Lower Inflammation

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
  • Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.
  • People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

Lower inflammation is associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

People who score higher in conscientiousness or extraversion tend to have lower levels of certain markers of inflammation.

Among the qualities that make up conscientiousness, being hardworking and organised stood out.

For extraversion, which includes both sociability and energy, the clearest result was for people who described themselves as active.

These patterns matter because inflammation that stays elevated over time is linked to both physical and psychological health.

Lower levels of long-term inflammation are linked to a lower risk of heart disease, stroke and premature death.

They have also been associated with less fatigue, a lower risk of depression and a slower decline in reasoning as people age.

The researchers pooled data from six studies involving more than 19,000 adults in the United States, England and Japan.

Participants rated how well words such as ‘organised’, ‘hardworking’ and ‘active’ described them.

The researchers then looked at how those answers related to two markers of inflammation in blood samples, C-reactive protein and interleukin-6.

Earlier research had already linked higher conscientiousness with lower levels of both inflammatory markers (Luchetti et al., 2014).

In this study, people who described themselves as organised or hardworking tended to have lower levels of both markers.

Being hardworking revealed the strongest association within conscientiousness, even stronger than the association for the overall trait score.

People who scored higher on extraversion tended to have lower C-reactive protein, and much of that association came from how active they remarked they were.

In fact, being active was more strongly associated with lower C-reactive protein than any other characteristic the researchers examined.

Being talkative indicated a small association in the opposite direction, while being lively was associated with lower levels of both inflammatory markers.

In several of the studies, the association with being active held up even after the researchers took other aspects of extraversion into account.

Being active and hardworking may both reflect how much energy people have for everyday tasks.

In earlier research, people who scored higher on the activity aspect of extraversion or the achievement-striving aspect of conscientiousness tended to have better aerobic capacity during a brisk walking test (Terracciano et al., 2013).

Regular physical activity could help explain part of the association with inflammation.

The relationship could run in the other direction, too, if people with higher inflammation feel less energetic and come to see themselves as less active or lively.

The study was published in the journal Psychoneuroendocrinology (Stephan et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Sources indicate that HAProxy is one of the most powerful open-source load balancers, widely used for its reliability, security, and performance. The Data Plane API adds a REST API to manage its configuration. Installing both by hand means a repository, a pinned package, a binary from GitHub, two config files and a systemd unit, on every load balancer.

This post walks through one Ansible playbook that does all of that, from the official HAProxy repositories, and gives the same result on every run.

The flow: add the repository → install HAProxy → write haproxy.cfg (first run only) → install the API binary → write its config → start the service.

Before running this playbook, ensure that:.

HAProxy has two kinds of stable branches:.

This playbook uses 3.3, the newest branch the PPA builds for Ubuntu 24.04 (3.4 LTS is only built for Ubuntu 26.04 and Debian 13). For a long-lived Ubuntu 24.04 install, set haproxy_version: "3.2" to stay on an LTS branch.

Below is the complete Ansible playbook to install and configure HAProxy along with the Data Plane API.

A minimal starting point. The parts the API needs:.

The playbook writes this file only once; after that the Data Plane API owns haproxy.cfg:.

The Data Plane API authenticates against the dataplaneapi userlist in haproxy.cfg. It also rewrites this file in its own normalized form every time it starts, so the template is written in exactly that form; otherwise every playbook run would report it as changed.

The playbook from this post, split into roles, plus Terraform code for the machine, is on GitHub: pderuiter/blog-haproxy-ansible. It creates an Ubuntu 24.04 VM and installs HAProxy and the Data Plane API exactly as above; set the API password in the vault and run ansible-playbook site.yml.

One playbook installs HAProxy and the Data Plane API the same way on every machine, and a version bump is a variable change.

#103530. Never IP:port — per-team CTF instances with frp, WireGuard and HMAC flags

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1564 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Never IP:port — per-team CTF instances with frp, WireGuard and HMAC flags

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a CTF where every web or pwn challenge is published as public-ip:port.
  • Sources indicate that that was the model we started from.
  • Recent findings suggest that NCTF26 is the 4th National CTF of Togo, organized by CERT.tg: an online qualifier (6 November 19:00 to 7 November 23:59 UTC), then a 24-hour on-site final in Lomé (19 November 11:40 to 20 November 11:40 UTC) for 10 teams and 47 players.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a CTF where every web or pwn challenge is published as public-ip:port. Two teammates launch the same challenge and step on each other's box. A player runs a port scan against the platform and lands on another team's instance. And on boot2root machines, where finding the services is the challenge, you have just handed out the answer in the connection string.

Sources indicate that that was the model we started from. This article is about the one we ended up running instead: one container per player, one flag per team, and a rule that no instance is ever reachable as IP:port.

Recent findings suggest that NCTF26 is the 4th National CTF of Togo, organized by CERT.tg: an online qualifier (6 November 19:00 to 7 November 23:59 UTC), then a 24-hour on-site final in Lomé (19 November 11:40 to 20 November 11:40 UTC) for 10 teams and 47 players. 609 challenges were played over the two phases. I was the technical lead. The public site is still up at https://ctf.tg; the cloud infrastructure was deleted on 21 November 2026.

In a recent development, the arena never exposes a challenge port to the internet. Each container publishes its port on the arena's loopback only, and the frp client opens an outbound tunnel to the front. Players only ever talk to the front.

Sources indicate that CTFd reaches the arena's Docker daemon through a filtering proxy, not a raw socket. That proxy only lets through the operations the instancer needs, keeps published ports on loopback, and refuses extra capabilities, sysctls and devices, with one narrow exception for the WireGuard gateway image. A web app that can create containers is a web app that can own the host; we treated that channel as the most sensitive part of the design.

The instancer is a CTFd plugin (about 2,400 lines of Python). From the player's side it comes down to four actions: launch, check status, renew, destroy.

Spawn. The plugin checks that the challenge is visible and its prerequisites are met, that the player is in a team, and that the per-team and global caps are not exceeded. It re-checks the caps after inserting the instance row, so two teammates clicking at the same time settle it without an SQL lock. Then it:.

Each box got 128 MiB of RAM, half a CPU and a 256-process limit by default, overridable per challenge up to a ceiling. An instance lived one hour and could be renewed five times. The global cap was 480 instances.

It has been revealed that one instance per (player, challenge), flag per team. In the first version, teammates shared one instance and kept getting in each other's way. On 29 October we switched to one box per player and kept the flag and the quota at team level. The per-team cap went from 4 to 6 between the qualifier and the final, because the Defense challenges keep a "production box" alive per team.

It has been revealed that reaper. A background thread, run by a single worker thanks to a file lock, passes every 30 seconds. It deletes expired instances, rows whose container vanished, labelled containers with no row, and stops a team's VPN gateway when the team has no VPN instance left.

A generic sketch of the spawn path, stripped of everything specific:.

Sources indicate that on 30 October, a week before the qualifier, we decided that instances would no longer be exposed as public IP:port. Three modes replaced it, chosen per challenge.

https. The simplest one. A wildcard certificate in front of nginx, and frp's HTTP vhost routes on the subdomain. With 80 random bits per label, you do not guess another team's instance.

Recent findings suggest that tls. For services that speak raw TCP, there is no Host header to route on. The SNI of the TLS handshake plays that role. The router terminates TLS with the same wildcard certificate, asks CTFd which private port the label maps to (an internal endpoint protected by a shared key, which answers an empty 404 on any failure), and pipes bytes. For the player:.

vpn. For machines where discovering services is part of the game, a subdomain does not help: it hides nothing about the ports. Each team gets its own WireGuard gateway container on the arena, its own Docker network and its own private /24. Instances in VPN mode get a fixed private IP; the player scans them like a lab.

The design goals were: no state to leak, nothing else reachable, and no per-player setup by an organizer.

Industry observers note that the client file is deliberately minimal: no DNS line, no default route. Only challenge traffic goes through the tunnel.

Because ping does not always cross the tunnel, the advice we drafted for players was a TCP scan without host discovery:.

According to recent reports, every instance challenge has a flag of type "team HMAC". Its content is just the challenge's slug. The flag is computed, never stored:.

According to recent reports, at submission, CTFd recomputes the expected flag for the submitting team and compares in constant time. Consequences we relied on:.

199 challenges used per-team flags during the qualifier.

The unsafe default was still the default. The code fell back to port mode when a challenge had no mode, or when the infrastructure for its mode was not configured, and it did so silently. Our import tool for creators' challenges never wrote the access mode. A dry run on 14 November, five days before the final, found the gap in the release strategy. On 15 November we classified the 46 challenges that still had no mode: 18 VPN, 10 HTTPS, 18 TLS. We fixed the data; the default itself was never changed. That is the first thing I would fix.

A proxy chain is not transparent. In https mode, nginx and frp route on Host, set their own X-Forwarded-* headers and normalize requests. Any challenge whose intended solve spoofs those headers, or relies on HTTP request smuggling, breaks. Four challenges had to move to tls between 15 and 17 November. We searched solvers and writeups for those headers, but a challenge without a text solver escapes that search; only replaying the solver through the player's URL catches it.

It has been revealed that A blocking lock under gevent. The frp configuration is edited under a file lock. The first version used a blocking flock. Under gevent, a second greenlet waiting on that lock froze its whole worker, and the holder could never release it. On 7 November that turned into 502s with the CPU at 0%. The fix was a non-blocking lock in a cooperative retry loop:.

That incident gets its own article in this series.

Industry observers note that frpc stopped answering reloads. The same day, the frp client, running for eight days, still answered "read config" but no longer "reload". Every spawn held the lock during a reload that never returned. A restart fixed it; from then on, a watcher probed reload latency every 3 minutes and alerted after two slow or failed probes in a row.

According to recent reports, orphan proxies. When removing a proxy failed, its block stayed in the config while the container was gone. The port went back to the pool, got reassigned, and the frp server refused the duplicate. We cleaned 33 orphans by hand. The reaper never learned to sweep proxies without a container.

Volumes leak. Containers were removed without their anonymous volumes. By 15 November the arena held 801 orphan volumes, 25.65 GB.

Entrypoints that ignore FLAG. Every "correct flag rejected" of the event had the same root cause: a creator's entrypoint that generated its own random flag, or a Dockerfile ENV that took precedence. Our pre-flight check confirmed that FLAG was in the environment, not that the file the player reads contained it. One of these surfaced mid-final. We fixed the image, but a flag read from the broken image could never be accepted: the team had to relaunch the instance and solve again. A related shell trap worth knowing:.

According to recent reports, the VPN lifecycle surprised players. The tunnel of a team only exists while it has at least one VPN instance. A player who connects WireGuard before launching anything has nothing in front of them. During the final, gateways were recreated several times an hour as teams released and destroyed boxes. The fix was an instruction to players, not code: launch first, then connect, and reconnect if the gateway was just recreated. And I only ran the complete player path (real client, handshake, HTTP 200, flag accepted) for the first time the night before the final. It worked, but that was luck, not process.

Again: loopback-only ports plus an outbound tunnel; random labels; a per-team VPN with derived keys and a firewall set before the interface; flags derived instead of stored; a filtering proxy in front of the Docker API; hard resource limits on every box.

This is part of NCTF26: running a national CTF. The next article is the post-mortem of the day the platform froze at 0% CPU. Results are on ctf.tg, the credits of every challenge author at ctf.tg/merci, community writeups at ctf.tg/writeups and ideas for NCTF27 at ctf.tg/idees.

Next in the series: CPU at 0% and 502s in a loop: how one blocking lock froze our national CTF platform.
